threat: Any MCP server that relays fetched-URL content, resource contents, or prompt-template text into a model-consumable field without stripping ANSI control bytes — an attacker who controls a URL or a writable record in a store the server reads can plant concealed instructions that the model follows while the human reviewer sees a benign response.
conditions: MCP server exposes a fetch-style tool OR a writable resource that later reads back into a model-consumable field. No sanitization of control bytes at the model-consumable boundary. Human reviewer relies on the rendered response rather than the raw bytes for approval. For stored variant: any write entrypoint (HTTP or MCP) reaches storage that a later MCP read surfaces.
mitigations: Strip ANSI escape sequences from any content before it enters a model-consumable field. Enforce URL allow-lists and input validation on write endpoints. Treat all external and stored text as untrusted the moment it can reach the model, regardless of protocol. Run raw-byte, field-path-anchored DAST against MCP surfaces continuously in CI, covering both direct-fetch and stored paths.
verify_note: All excerpts verified verbatim from mrscan-batch10-2.txt lines 20, 31-35, 44-46, and 49.

title: Agent skill security is a lifecycle problem, not just a runtime one (SkillSec-Eval)
summary: Reusable agent 'skills' are a new supply-chain unit, but security work has mostly looked at prompt injection and runtime execution. SkillSec-Eval maps threats across the whole skill lifecycle — repository admission, semantic retrieval, planner selection, execution, and skill evolution — and, over 327 real skills, shows vulnerabilities appear at stages well before execution.

lessons.point: Skill security today is scoped too narrowly — it fixates on prompt injection and runtime, leaving the rest of the skill lifecycle unexamined.
lessons.excerpt: existing security research primarily focuses on prompt injection and runtime execution, leaving security risks throughout the broader skill lifecycle largely unexplored

lessons.point: A useful threat model spans five lifecycle stages, so a skill scanner should check admission, retrieval, and planner-selection risks, not only execution.
lessons.excerpt: a threat taxonomy spanning repository admission, semantic retrieval, planner selection, execution, and skill evolution

lessons.point: Empirically, across 327 real-world skills, vulnerabilities show up at multiple stages beyond execution — so lifecycle-aware analysis is needed, not just a runtime guard.
lessons.excerpt: vulnerabilities arise at multiple lifecycle stages beyond execution

takeaway: When you scan or admit agent skills, cover the whole lifecycle (admission, retrieval, planner selection, evolution) — a runtime-only check misses where most of the risk actually lives.
prior_art: OpenClaw/ClawHub agentic supply-chain and MCP tool-poisoning work cover parts of this; the novel delta is the explicit lifecycle taxonomy (five stages) plus an empirical study over 327 real skills rather than a single attack demo.
verify_note: Independent verifier: all three lessons match the abstract; no fabricated attack/defense specifics.

domain: MCP server security / agentic AWS access
title: AWS API MCP Server fails open: security policy is silently bypassed for the process lifetime when startup init fails (CVE-2026-16584)
summary: The AWS API MCP Server (awslabs.aws-api-mcp-server) loads the data needed to enforce its configured deny/gate security policy at process startup. If that load fails, the server keeps running with no enforcement in place, so the per-request security check is skipped for the entire life of the process and AWS operations the policy was meant to restrict execute unchecked. This is a fail-open (CWE-455) design flaw that turns a transient startup error into a durable, silent policy bypass on an agent's path to real AWS infrastructure.

lessons.point: Security enforcement that depends on data loaded at startup must fail closed: if the policy data can't load, the server should refuse to serve rather than run unguarded.
lessons.excerpt: If that load fails, the server continues running without the enforcement data in place.

lessons.point: The bypass is not per-request but persistent — once a process starts with a failed init, every subsequent request skips the deny/gate rules until the process is restarted successfully.
lessons.excerpt: the per-request security check is then bypassed for the lifetime of the process: configured deny and gate rules are not consulted

lessons.point: The failure is attacker-influenceable: startup during degraded connectivity or adverse conditions can cause the policy data load to fail, yielding an unrestricted server after restart.
lessons.excerpt: Triggering startup during degraded connectivity or adverse conditions causing policy data load failures

lessons.point: Least-privilege IAM credentials are the correct defense-in-depth: the MCP policy layer is not the only control, and scoping the underlying AWS credentials limits blast radius when the policy layer fails.
lessons.excerpt: Use least-privilege IAM credentials as interim mitigation

takeaway: An MCP server's in-app allow/deny policy is worthless as a security boundary if a startup load failure makes it silently fail open — enforce fail-closed and always back it with least-privilege credentials.
prior_art: CWE-455 (Non-exit on Failed Initialization) fail-open patterns generally, and MCP enforcement-layer bypass cases like the ToolHive SSRF; no known prior case of an MCP agent security policy silently failing open for the process lifetime on failed startup init.
threat: An AI agent using the AWS API MCP server can execute AWS CLI operations that the configured deny/gate policy was meant to block, because a failed startup init silently disables enforcement for the whole process — enabling privilege escalation and unauthorized infrastructure changes within the credentials' scope.
conditions: Server version >= 0.2.13 and < 1.3.47; Startup-time policy/enforcement data load fails (e.g. degraded connectivity or adverse startup conditions); Server continues running instead of exiting; agent then issues AWS operations the policy intended to restrict
mitigations: Upgrade to awslabs.aws-api-mcp-server 1.3.47 or later; Scope the AWS credentials the server uses to least privilege (IAM); Ensure stable connectivity/dependencies during server startup and monitor for init failures; Design MCP/tool policy layers to fail closed and assert policy presence before serving requests
verify_note: All four lessons match the GHSA/CVE-2026-16584 advisory verbatim or faithfully; only the 'attacker-influenceable' framing is mildly overstated (advisory cites degraded connectivity as a cause, CVSS vector is Local), not enough to refute.

title: Provider safety guardrails blocked incident response during the Hugging Face agentic intrusion
author: Johann Rehberger
summary: Hugging Face disclosed an intrusion it says was driven end to end by an autonomous AI agent. By its own account a malicious dataset gave code execution, after which the agent took host access, harvested cloud/cluster credentials and moved laterally, logging 17,000+ events; HF did not publish exploit details or IOCs, and none of it is independently corroborated. The sharpest lesson is the response: HF says it first tried frontier models behind commercial APIs and provider safety guardrails repeatedly blocked the forensic workload, forcing a pivot to a locally hosted open-weight model.

lessons.point: Vendor safety guardrails blocked forensic analysis of attacker payloads and commands via commercial APIs mid-incident, forcing a pivot to a local open-weight model - treat provider refusal as an IR availability risk.
lessons.excerpt: initially tried to use frontier models behind commercial APIs, but provider safety guardrails repeatedly blocked the forensic workload

lessons.point: Stage a locally deployable open-weight model as a forensic fallback BEFORE an incident - procuring one under fire is not a plan. Local execution also keeps attacker data and credentials inside your environment.
lessons.excerpt: it is probably a good idea to vet and stage a locally deployable open-weight model before an incident occurs, not during one

lessons.point: Agentic intrusions reuse familiar TTPs - the delta defenders must absorb is velocity and scale, not novel exploitation.
lessons.excerpt: the exploits and TTPs will be quite familiar at first, but the velocity and scale of agentic adversaries is something defenders need to adapt to

threat: An autonomous agent framework establishes a beachhead via a malicious dataset, escalates to node-level access, harvests cloud and cluster credentials, and moves laterally at machine speed.
conditions: A model/dataset hub that executes remote dataset-loader code and templates from untrusted uploads; defenders relying on commercial model APIs for forensic analysis. Note: the intrusion narrative is Hugging Face's own account; exploit details and IOCs were not published.
mitigations: Vet and pre-stage a self-hosted open-weight model for forensics; keep an LLM-based anomaly triager (HF's flagged the intrusion first); rotate tokens and review account activity.
takeaway: Assume your commercial AI provider may refuse to help you during a breach - pre-stage a local open-weight forensic model the same way you pre-stage backups.
prior_art: Guardrails obstructing legitimate security and malware analysis is a long-running, frequently-reported community complaint, and the intrusion TTPs themselves are conventional. The delta is a fresh, concrete, named instance - a vendor pivoting to a self-hosted open-weight model mid-incident - not a new phenomenon.
verify_note: Independent verifier: removed an invented causal claim (that exploit-gen and forensic refusals are the same mechanism); hedged the intrusion narrative as HF's own uncorroborated account; novelty 74->45 (guardrails-block-security-work is a known complaint).

editorial.reason: A disclosed real-world incident (the Hugging Face agentic intrusion) with an actionable IR lesson: pre-stage a local open-weight forensic model because commercial guardrails may refuse the workload mid-breach.

title: Insecure coding preferences persist in LLM long-term memory and resist normal correction
author: Yuchen Chen et al.
summary: Across four LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, Qwen, Grok) and five languages, storing insecure coding preferences in long-term memory raised vulnerable-code generation by 2.7-50.3 percentage points, and those memories proved hard to overwrite through ordinary conversation. Warning rates lagged vulnerability rates by 5.4-14.0 pp, so the model gets less safe faster than it gets more cautious - and only memory-level filtering restored baseline behavior. Scope: this is LLM-based code generation with persistent memory, not autonomous tool-using agents.

lessons.point: Long-term memory is a persistent, cross-session attack surface: once an insecure preference is stored it silently steers later security-critical generations.
lessons.excerpt: once insecure coding preferences are stored, they may silently influence security-critical decisions in subsequent generations

lessons.point: You cannot reliably talk a poisoned memory out of the system - the effect survives rephrasing and normal interaction.
lessons.excerpt: insecure memories are difficult to overwrite through normal interactions and can broadly influence model outputs even when prompts are phrased differently

lessons.point: Filter at the memory layer, not the prompt layer: memory-level filtering reached a 100% detection rate on the authors' own evaluated set of risky memory entries (not validated against unseen or adversarial memory content) and restored the no-memory baseline, while prompt-level fixes cost up to 15.9 pp of functional correctness.
lessons.excerpt: memory-level safety filtering achieves a 100\% detection rate on our evaluated risky memory entries and restores generation behavior to the without-memory baseline

threat: An attacker or careless user plants an insecure preference in an LLM's long-term memory, durably degrading the security of code it later generates.
conditions: Any coding assistant with cross-session persistent memory that stores user preferences without validating them.
mitigations: Screen entries at write time to memory; treat stored preferences as untrusted input on read; prefer memory-level filtering over appending security requirements to prompts, which costs correctness.
takeaway: Validate what goes into LLM memory - a poisoned preference outlives the conversation and can't be argued away.
prior_art: Memory and context poisoning is an active area and RAG poisoning is well studied; this extends known memory-poisoning concepts rather than introducing a new primitive. The delta is a quantified measurement specific to stored *coding preferences* plus the risk-warning gap and the memory-vs-prompt mitigation comparison. The authors describe it as the first systematic study of this - their own characterization, not independently verified. Accepted to ISSTA 2026.
verify_note: Independent verifier: dropped the unsupported 'agent' framing (source is LLM code generation with memory); scoped the 100% detection rate to the authors' own evaluated entries; attributed the 'first study' claim; novelty 76->50.

title: AWS Bedrock AgentCore Python SDK: argument-delimiter injection in install_packages() gives RCE in the Code Interpreter sandbox (CVE-2026-16796)
summary: The AWS Bedrock AgentCore Python SDK (bedrock-agentcore) exposes a Code Interpreter client whose install_packages() method builds a pip invocation from caller-supplied package names without neutralizing argument delimiters (CWE-88). A crafted package specifier can smuggle extra pip options/arguments, so a remote authenticated user who can influence those arguments — including via model-generated output routed into the installer — can execute arbitrary commands inside the managed sandbox. Fixed in 1.18.1; CVSS 8.4 High.

lessons.point: Package-name arguments flow into a pip command line without delimiter neutralization, letting a crafted specifier inject additional pip options/arguments (classic CWE-88 argument injection).
lessons.excerpt: Improper neutralization of argument delimiters in the install_packages() method

lessons.point: The injection yields arbitrary command execution inside the Code Interpreter sandbox, not just unwanted package installs — an authenticated user who controls the arguments gets code execution.
lessons.excerpt: A remote authenticated user who can influence the arguments to install_packages() can execute arbitrary commands within the Code Interpreter sandbox environment.

lessons.point: In an agent runtime the 'authenticated user who influences arguments' is often the LLM itself; the documented workaround is to never pass untrusted or model-generated input to install_packages().
lessons.excerpt: do not pass untrusted or model-generated input to install_packages()

lessons.point: Remediation is upgrade to 1.18.1, or validate dynamic package names against strict PyPI naming conventions before invoking the SDK.
lessons.excerpt: Validate dynamic package names against strict PyPI naming conventions before invoking the SDK.

takeaway: In agent SDKs, any helper that shells out (pip install, git, curl) from model- or user-influenced arguments is an RCE sink unless argument delimiters are neutralized — treat install_packages() and similar as a command boundary.
prior_art: Generic CWE-88 argument-delimiter injection (historic pip/git argument-injection bugs) plus the well-known 'LLM output reaching a shell-out sink = RCE' class; this is a concrete named instance in the AWS Bedrock AgentCore SDK.
threat: A remote authenticated caller — or the agent's own LLM output routed into install_packages() — smuggles pip options via a crafted package specifier to run arbitrary commands inside the managed Code Interpreter sandbox, breaking the sandbox's confidentiality/integrity boundary.
conditions: Using AWS Bedrock AgentCore Python SDK (bedrock-agentcore) < 1.18.1; Code Interpreter client's install_packages() is reachable with attacker- or model-influenced package arguments; Attacker is authenticated / can influence the argument values
mitigations: Upgrade bedrock-agentcore to >= 1.18.1; Do not pass untrusted or model-generated input to install_packages(); Validate package names against strict PyPI naming conventions and reject option-like tokens before invoking the SDK; Prefer argv-list invocation with a '--' end-of-options separator over string-built command lines
verify_note: novelty disagreement (analyst 68 vs verifier 47); Advisory confirms package name, CVE-2026-16796, CVSS 8.4, CWE-88, fix 1.18.1, and workaround verbatim; all four lessons faithfully reflect the source, though the underlying lesson is a known vuln class applied to a fresh SDK.

title: Salience Induction: steering a multi-hop RAG agent to the wrong answer using only true statements and no instructions
summary: A preprint attacks agentic RAG through what the authors call the salience channel - position, emphasis, framing and semantic proximity - with edits that keep every retrieved claim true and inject no directives. Self-reported results on the authors' own benchmark: 83.3% attack success under a 30% edit budget, with the strongest baseline defense still leaving 75.7%. The teachable part is the stealth axis, not the efficiency axis: a 30% edit budget is generous, but factuality auditing and instruction filtering have nothing to catch.

lessons.point: Two controls many RAG deployments lean on - verify retrieved claims are factual, strip instruction-like text from context - are aimed at the wrong channel. An attack that only reorders and reframes true facts passes both by construction.
lessons.excerpt: We identify a third attack surface: the salience channel, through which fact position, emphasis, framing, and semantic proximity can redirect reasoning even when all retrieved claims are true and no instructions are present.

lessons.point: Read the numbers as an upper bound in a favorable setting: self-reported, on a benchmark the same team built, with an optimizer in the loop, at a 30% edit budget whose unit is unspecified. The honest claim is that the strongest evaluated defense barely moved the needle, not that the attack is cheap.
lessons.excerpt: Under a 30% edit budget, Salience Induction achieves an 83.3% attack success rate; the strongest evaluated baseline defense leaves 75.7% post-defense ASR.

lessons.point: The defense direction is input-side normalization rather than content filtering - canonicalize order, emphasis and formatting of retrieved evidence before it reaches the model. A cheap version you can run today without this paper: permutation-stability testing, i.e. re-ask with the evidence shuffled and flag answers that change.
lessons.excerpt: Our lightweight input-side defense, Salience Normalization, reduces attack success to 15.3% under standard attacks and 23.6% under an adaptive attack.

takeaway: If an attacker can edit your corpus without lying, factuality checks and injection filters both return clean - order and emphasis are attacker-controlled state.
threat: An adversary with write access to a retrieval corpus redirects multi-hop attribute binding using only truth-preserving edits, defeating factuality and instruction-filter defenses.
conditions: Attacker can edit a meaningful fraction of retrieved evidence (the paper reports results at a 30% edit budget; no lower-budget sweep is given).
mitigations: Input-side salience normalization; permutation-stability testing; provenance weighting of evidence rather than treating retrieved passages as interchangeable.
prior_art: PoisonedRAG and corpus-content poisoning (inject false facts) and indirect prompt injection (inject directives) - this paper's delta is dropping both. Against 'Lost in the Middle' and distractor-robustness work the delta is thinner: position and distractor sensitivity are well-replicated properties, and this weaponizes them. Nearest pool entry: the archived 'RAG poisoning via injected malicious documents in the retrieval corpus'.
verify_note: Verifier scored novelty 45, arguing the salience channel largely reduces to known context-position/distractor effects and that 'a third attack surface' oversells; it also caught two overstatements now fixed (the strongest baseline does reduce ASR by ~7.6 points, so 'defenses do not catch them' was wrong; and the five-model/three-architecture generalization applies to the attack, not to the defense figures). Held for review on novelty disagreement.

title: (A)iSpy: the trojan moves from the model file into the ML runtime - authors report it amplifies weak poisoning to 100% backdoor success
summary: An arXiv preprint proposes (A)iSpy, a trojan that lives in the ML execution environment (a PoC in ONNX Runtime's training and inference engines) rather than in the data or the model artifact. From inside the computation graph it watches transient tensor state and acts on it: the authors report it amplifies a separately-delivered, otherwise-ineffective data poison from near-zero to 100% backdoor success, and covertly exfiltrates training hyperparameters through the model's own weights or output logits. Evidence is abstract-only and self-reported - the value here is the threat model, not the numbers.

lessons.point: Your ML supply-chain audit probably stops at the artifact. The authors' framing premise is that data and model files get scanned or integrity-checked while third-party graph-compilation and hardware-acceleration libraries - the layer that actually executes the model - are implicitly trusted.
lessons.excerpt: While current practices audit data and model artifacts or rely on file integrity checks, the execution environment remains implicitly trusted.

lessons.point: A runtime implant is interesting as a force multiplier, not a standalone backdoor: it lets an attacker split the attack across two individually weak footholds (a poisoned-data trickle plus a runtime module), which is also the precondition that limits it - you need both.
lessons.excerpt: by observing steganographic triggers, it transforms otherwise weak data poisoning into effective backdoor attacks, increasing success rates from near zero to 100%

lessons.point: The same position yields a confidentiality channel that leaves through artifacts you intend to publish - the authors report exfiltrating training hyperparameters via model weights or output logits. Treat the paired evasion claim as unassessable: the abstract names no scanner or backdoor-detection method it defeats.
lessons.excerpt: the Trojan identifies all critical training hyperparameters and covertly exfiltrates them via model weights or output logits

takeaway: If you attest models but not the runtime that executes them, your provenance chain has a hole the size of ONNX Runtime.
threat: A malicious or compromised third-party ML runtime module observes live training/inference and manipulates it, evading data- and model-artifact-level auditing entirely.
conditions: Attacker can ship a modified runtime/acceleration library into the victim's ML pipeline; for the backdoor-amplification result, also a low-rate data poisoning foothold.
mitigations: Pin and attest runtime dependencies; SBOM coverage for inference engines; run training in an environment whose libraries are provenance-verified rather than pulled at build time.
prior_art: Bagdasaryan & Shmatikov, 'Blind Backdoors in Deep Learning Models' (USENIX Security 2021) - malicious training-pipeline code that observes live training and synthesizes a backdoor without touching the dataset; ImpNet (2022) - backdoors injected at compile time, invisible in data and model artifacts; Song et al. (CCS 2017) - exfiltrating training secrets through model weights. Nearest pool entry: ShadowPickle, which covers the model-artifact scanning layer this work deliberately steps past.
verify_note: Verifier confirmed every claim traces to the abstract but scored novelty far lower (42), naming Blind Backdoors and ImpNet as covering the core 'untrusted execution substrate' idea years earlier; it also flagged that all figures are abstract-only, self-reported, and that the evasion claim names no defense it defeats. Held for review on novelty disagreement and evidence level.

title: Apple fixed the macOS Terminal ANSI DNS-exfiltration sink used to chain prompt injection
author: Johann Rehberger
summary: A prompt injection hidden in a spreadsheet cell made an LLM CLI tool emit ANSI escape codes that macOS Terminal interpreted as a DNS request, exfiltrating data from other rows with no tool or shell call involved. Reported to Apple in December 2024 and fixed in macOS Tahoe 26.1 (3 November 2025). The flaw spans two rendering-layer components, neither of them the model: the terminal emulator's escape-sequence handling (now patched) and CLI tools that pass model output to the terminal unencoded (still unaddressed industry-wide).

lessons.point: Rendering model output is itself a sink - data can leave without the agent ever invoking a tool, shell command, or MCP call.
lessons.excerpt: An attacker does not necessarily need to trigger a function, shell command, skill, or MCP tool to cause data leakage or other harm.

lessons.point: LLM-integrated CLIs should encode control characters by default (caret notation, like `cat -v`) and make raw terminal output an explicit opt-in.
lessons.excerpt: CLI tools should safely encode control characters by default, using an approach similar to `cat -v`. Raw terminal output should require explicit opt-in.

lessons.point: The injection tolerated an author error (BEL described as ASCII 10 rather than 7) and still worked - in-context instructions degrade gracefully, so near-miss payloads are not safe.
lessons.excerpt: That was my mistake in the prompt, but it did not prevent the in-context learning instruction from working.

threat: Untrusted content processed by an LLM CLI causes the model to emit ANSI escape sequences that the terminal emulator acts on, exfiltrating data over DNS.
conditions: An LLM-integrated CLI that passes model output to the terminal unencoded, on a terminal emulator that acts on escape sequences (macOS Terminal before Tahoe 26.1).
mitigations: Update to macOS Tahoe 26.1+ for the emulator half; independently, encode control characters in your CLI's output by default - the author flags this as the still-unfixed half. Treat model output as untrusted data at every rendering boundary.
takeaway: Sanitize model output at the rendering boundary - both the terminal emulator and your CLI's own output path are execution surfaces, and only the former got patched.
prior_art: Every primitive was already established: the ANSI-DNS behavior by David Leadbeater (2023), LLMs emitting ANSI escapes by Leon Derczynski, and the author's own Terminal DiLLMa research (2024). This is disclosure-closure - the marginal contribution is the full chained PoC and the resulting Apple fix, not a new technique.
verify_note: Independent verifier: the flaw spans two rendering components (terminal emulator, patched; CLI output encoding, unpatched), not one sink; prior-art attribution confirmed accurate; novelty 48->40.

title: Self-state attacks: corrupting an agent's own memory and config uses legitimate syscalls
author: Yimeng Chen et al.
summary: Self-hosted agents read and write their own memory and configuration files, so once an attacker can write to that state the corruption itself is performed with legitimate OS system calls - the malicious step does not look anomalous at the OS layer. The authors formalize a four-axis attack space, realize 43 operations on real self-state files injected into traces from a representative self-hosted agent, and find a layered defense covers most cells with a small residual that stays structurally indistinguishable. Note the precondition: this assumes the attacker already has local write access; the paper does not address how that access is obtained.

lessons.point: Given an attacker who can already write to an agent's state files, the corruption step is performed with legitimate system calls - so the malicious action itself carries no distinguishing OS-level signal. This is a post-compromise finding, not a new access path.
lessons.excerpt: An agent may get compromised via corruption of its own state -- a compromise realized via legitimate OS system call invocation.

lessons.point: Layer the defense by state type: access-control prevention on instruction and configuration layers, workload-conditioned detection on the memory layer, periodic backup for recovery.
lessons.excerpt: a layered defense stack (access-control prevention on the instruction and configuration layers, workload-conditioned detection on the memory layer, and periodic backup for recovery) is effective on most attack cells

lessons.point: For a small residual subset of attack cells, OS-level signals alone are structurally insufficient to separate malicious from legitimate state changes - even though the layered stack handles most cells. Plan for recovery, not prevention alone.
lessons.excerpt: a small residual attack surface remains structurally indistinguishable at the OS level

threat: An attacker with write access to an agent's instruction, configuration, or memory files redirects its behavior persistently, without exploiting the agent or the OS.
conditions: Self-hosted agents persisting memory and configuration to the local filesystem, AND an attacker who has already obtained local write access to those files (e.g. via prior code execution).
mitigations: Apply mandatory access control to instruction/config files, use workload-conditioned detection on memory files, and take periodic backups so recovery is possible for the undetectable residual.
takeaway: Treat an agent's memory and config files as protected assets with their own access-control and backup policy - once an attacker can write them, the corruption step itself looks legitimate.
prior_art: Agent memory poisoning and config tampering have been discussed piecemeal. The contribution is systematizing the space (four-axis, 23-cell matrix) and measuring which cells OS defenses cover - not a new attack capability, since it presumes existing local write access. 'Self-state attacks' is the authors' own coinage in this paper. Preprint, not peer-reviewed.
verify_note: Independent verifier: surfaced the unstated precondition - the attacker must already hold local write access, making this post-compromise systematization rather than a new access path; 'representative' agent not 'real'; novelty 73->45.

editorial.reason: Part of the live agent-security cluster with a directly actionable hardening step: apply access-control and backup to an agent's own memory/config files.

title: Scientific computing in the age of agentic AI
summary: OpenAI's field report on eight agent-assisted scientific-computing projects (five using Codex only, three combining Codex and Claude Code, primarily in life sciences) reports a consistent pattern: agents shift the human's job from implementation to verification and orchestration — defining what to build, specifying how to measure correctness, and deciding when a project ships. The security-relevant lessons are (a) agents express confidence even on clearly wrong output, so groundedness has to come from an external reference (parity with an existing tool, simulated data with known answers, statistical checks), (b) initial implementations are fast but resolving edge cases and numerical differences dominates elapsed time, and (c) lower implementation cost fragments maintainership — today's rewrite is tomorrow's abandoned code without an explicit steward. The transferable claim for agent harness design is that verification-side infra (acceptance tests, reference outputs, iterative benchmarks) is the actual bottleneck once agents are cheap.
takeaway: Once agents are cheap, verification is the bottleneck: acceptance tests, parity references, and named maintainers are the new critical infrastructure — not more agent capability.

lessons.point: Agents produce confident-sounding output that contains clear errors; the strongest defense is an external reference with a measurable acceptance target — parity with an existing tool, simulated data with pre-computed answers, or bounded statistical behavior.
lessons.excerpt: agents handled specific, well-scoped requests effectively but could not reliably judge whether their work was scientifically valid or met expectations. Indeed, agents often expressed confidence even when their work contained clear errors. Human reviewers therefore needed to find reliable ways to validate the results. The strongest approaches used an external reference or measurable acceptance target such as exact output agreement, parity with an existing tool, appropriate statistical behavior, or answers established in advance using simulated data.

lessons.point: The role shift is verification/orchestration, not authoring: humans set the goal, define correctness metrics, and gate ship — a re-partitioning that dictates where evaluation infra has to live in an agent-assisted org.
lessons.excerpt: Contributors consistently describe a shift in the researchers’ role from implementation to verification and orchestration: specifying what to build, defining how to measure correctness, and deciding when a project is ready to ship.

lessons.point: The last-mile is where the elapsed time actually sits: fast first implementations, slow edge-case and numerical-diff resolution — an argument against benchmarking agents on first-pass throughput and for benchmarking on time-to-ship-quality.
lessons.excerpt: Agents often produced initial implementations quickly, but resolving edge cases and subtle numerical differences took much longer. Completing the “last mile” of an implementation often took the most work.

lessons.point: Cheap agents create a maintainership fragmentation problem: rewrites split communities and expert attention, so a rewrite without a named owner and credible maintenance plan is a future abandonment liability.
lessons.excerpt: But lower implementation costs also make it easier to produce many similar rewrites, fragmenting users and spreading the expert attention required to keep any one tool reliable. That makes long-term stewardship and attribution essential.

actionable.title: Verification-first harness pattern for agent-assisted engineering work
actionable.detail: Codify the OpenAI field-report pattern for any team standing up an agent-assisted engineering loop: (1) before any agent runs, define an external reference — parity target, simulated dataset with known answers, or bounded statistical property — that will actually decide 'ship or not', (2) break the goal into small feedback-driven iterations with intermediate benchmarks so the agent's confident-but-wrong pattern gets caught early, (3) explicitly assign a human owner for last-mile edge cases (numerical diffs, format oddities) because the field-report data says this dominates elapsed time, and (4) attach a maintenance/stewardship plan at the same moment you commit the rewrite — no rewrite without a named owner and a credible support line, or it becomes future abandoned code.

prior_art: First-party OpenAI messaging on agentic coding productivity has been ongoing across 2026. The delta of this specific report is the eight-project retrospective corpus (five Codex-only, three Codex+Claude Code), the explicit naming of verification acceptance patterns (parity, simulated-answer, statistical), and the stewardship / abandonment framing. The verification-bottleneck claim overlaps with the pool's 'human review catches agent PR risk' claim and PortSwigger's HTTP Terminator human-in-cascade pattern.
verify_note: All four excerpts verified verbatim against data/_raw/mrscan-batch09-2.txt; related_claims exist in data/claims.json. This is a first-party OpenAI capability report, not a security incident — threat/conditions/mitigations left null and populated the ai-research/harness angle instead.

title: TensorZero Gateway: a request parameter that overrides the server's object-storage config gives arbitrary file read and SSRF
summary: TensorZero's /internal/object_storage endpoint accepted a caller-supplied storage_path that dynamically overrode the gateway's configured object-storage backend. Selecting the filesystem backend turns it into arbitrary file read; selecting s3_compatible turns it into SSRF toward internal and cloud-metadata endpoints. Textbook bug class, worth logging only because LLM gateways keep shipping optional auth alongside endpoints whose /internal prefix is doing the authorization.

lessons.point: The bug class is 'the caller picks the backend': whenever a request field selects a storage driver or endpoint, the caller has inherited a server-side trust decision, and the two sinks are always the same - local file read and outbound SSRF.
lessons.excerpt: The `/internal/object_storage` endpoint accepts a caller-supplied JSON `storage_path` parameter that dynamically overrides the TensorZero `[object_storage]` configuration.

lessons.point: A path prefix is not an authorization boundary. `/internal` only means internal if something enforces it; here exposure hinges entirely on whether the operator turned authentication on.
lessons.excerpt: If a developer's TensorZero deployment has authentication enabled, only authenticated callers can exploit this vulnerability.

lessons.point: Durable control for anyone running an LLM gateway: default-deny egress from the gateway to link-local and RFC1918 ranges, so a storage-backend confusion bug cannot reach cloud metadata even when it exists.
lessons.excerpt: the caller can coerce the gateway into making outbound object storage requests to attacker-chosen internal/cloud-metadata endpoints

takeaway: LLM gateways are ordinary web services with an unusual amount of credentials on disk - audit them for caller-selectable backends before anything AI-specific.
threat: An untrusted caller reads gateway-local credential files or pivots to internal/cloud-metadata services through the gateway.
conditions: Gateway reachable by untrusted callers; the advisory states exploitation is limited to authenticated callers where authentication is enabled.
mitigations: Upgrade to 2026.6.0; block external access to /internal/object_storage; enable gateway authentication; restrict egress.
prior_art: Caller-controlled S3-compatible endpoint override -> SSRF (repeatedly patched in MinIO-integrating and self-hosted file services); CWE-73 external control of file path via selectable storage driver; Capital One-era cloud-metadata SSRF; Spring Boot Actuator /env config-override exposure. The only new facts are the product, endpoint and version.
verify_note: Verifier scored novelty 12/100 - 'the conceptual delta over prior art is approximately zero', same primitive, sinks, fix and workaround as a decade of prior bugs, and it does not even carry the LLM-specific wrinkle (no prompt-injection-reachable path). Also corrected: the advisory says files that MAY contain credentials, does not demonstrate metadata retrieval, states exposure as a precondition rather than an observed fact, and gives no CVE/CVSS/affected range. Held for review as derivative.

title: AsyncAPI npm compromise: import-time payload defeats --ignore-scripts
summary: Attackers backdoored five @asyncapi npm versions that execute at module-load (import/require) time rather than via a postinstall hook, so `npm install --ignore-scripts` doesn't stop them. They didn't compromise npm directly: a `pull_request_target` pwn request exposed the project's bot token (PAT), after which the project's own trusted-publishing (GitHub OIDC) pipeline shipped the poisoned packages with valid provenance attestations.

lessons.point: The payload runs at import time, not install time — so the standard --ignore-scripts defense is irrelevant; the trigger is require()/import, not a lifecycle hook.
lessons.excerpt: Because the trigger is an import rather than an install script

lessons.point: Hook-focused scanners miss this entirely because the packages declare no preinstall/postinstall hooks at all.
lessons.excerpt: Security tooling that focuses on preinstall/postinstall auditing will not flag these packages.

lessons.point: Trusted publishing / provenance did NOT prevent the attack: valid OIDC attestations were produced from unauthorized commits, so a green provenance check is not proof of a trustworthy release.
lessons.excerpt: The attestations accurately identified the legitimate repositories, commits, and workflows that created the packages, even though the triggering commits were unauthorized.

threat: A poisoned transitive dependency runs attacker code on any workstation, CI runner, or container build that imports it, with no install script required.
mitigations: Pin/lock and vet dependency updates by content (not just provenance); treat import-time behavior as executable; segment CI credentials; audit pull_request_target workflows that check out untrusted PR code.
takeaway: Import-time malware makes --ignore-scripts useless and a valid provenance attestation is not a trust signal when the pipeline itself is hijacked.
prior_art: The 2025 Shai-Hulud / npm postinstall-worm campaigns and the related @mastra scope takeover — same 'compromise a maintainer/bot identity' root cause, but those triggered on install hooks; the novel delta here is import-time execution plus abuse of trusted-publishing provenance.
verify_note: Independent verifier: claims supported; softened token-theft to 'exposed PAT' per source hedge.

title: The npm Threat Landscape: Attack Surface and Mitigations
summary: Unit 42's rolling ledger of the post-Shai-Hulud npm compromise era. Since the September 2025 self-replicating worm, adversary TTPs have shifted along three axes: wormable propagation via stolen npm/GitHub PATs, infrastructure-level persistence via CI/CD embed, and multi-stage dormant payloads that evade scanners. The dossier documents Bitwarden CLI (April 2026), SAP @cap-js (April 29), TanStack (May 11 — first case of a worm publishing packages with valid SLSA Build Level 3 provenance via OIDC token extraction from /proc/<Runner.Worker>/mem), @antv (May 19, 639 malicious versions in one hour), @redhat-cloud-services (June 1, 32 packages with valid SLSA provenance), and AsyncAPI (July 14, unprotected pre-production release branches exploited). Notably: on July 14, GitHub Copilot's automated dependency loading imported a trojanized @asyncapi/specs@6.11.2 on a developer machine — 'the developer did not run npm install manually. The tooling did it for them.'
takeaway: npm supply-chain risk is a continuously advancing threat landscape, not a series of point incidents; SLSA provenance is necessary but not sufficient because it certifies the pipeline built the artifact — not that the pipeline's internal state was clean.

lessons.point: SLSA Build Level 3 provenance is now confirmed-bypassable: a worm can publish signed packages with valid attestations because provenance only certifies which pipeline built the artifact, not that the pipeline's state was clean when it built.
lessons.excerpt: This is the first documented case of a worm publishing malicious npm packages with valid SLSA Build Level 3 provenance. Sigstore correctly attested that the packages were built by release.yml from refs/heads/main of TanStack/router — because they were. SLSA provenance confirms which pipeline built a package, not whether that pipeline's internal state was clean.

lessons.point: The GitHub Actions cache is a poisonable pivot: actions/cache@v5 saves with a runner-internal token that is not gated by workflow permissions, and a fork's pull_request_target run can pre-compute the exact key a later release workflow will hit.
lessons.excerpt: The fork's code wrote a 1.1 GB poisoned pnpm store under the exact cache key that release.yml would later look up. The key was pre-computed from the public pnpm-lock.yaml using the same hashFiles() formula the workflow uses. The poisoned cache entry then sat dormant for eight hours. A critical detail: actions/cache@v5's post-job save uses a runner-internal token, not the workflow GITHUB_TOKEN, so setting permissions: contents: read on the workflow does not prevent the cache write.

lessons.point: AI coding assistants are already the delivery mechanism: on a compromised macOS machine, Copilot's automatic dependency load pulled the trojanized package — the human never typed npm install.
lessons.excerpt: On July 14, 2026, Unit 42 researchers analyzed a compromised macOS developer machine on which the developer opened a project workspace in GitHub Copilot. When the copilot parsed the workspace and triggered automated dependency loading, it imported the trojanized @asyncapi/specs@6.11.2 package. This silently launched the Stage-1 loader, which fetched Miasma sync.js from IPFS and spawned it under Homebrew Node.js v22, initiating active beaconing to 85.137.53[.]71:8080. The developer did not run npm install manually. The tooling did it for them.

lessons.point: --ignore-scripts is a partial control: preinstall hooks are only one delivery path, and a bin field can re-arm the payload the next time the user or any script invokes the compromised binary name (bw in the Bitwarden case).
lessons.excerpt: Since the legitimate Bitwarden CLI also uses bw as its binary name, this serves as a secondary trigger. Even if preinstall is blocked (e.g., via --ignore-scripts), the malware executes the next time the user or any script invokes bw.

actionable.title: Treat AI coding-assistant dependency loads as CI/CD-scope events and gate them accordingly
actionable.detail: Because Copilot/Cursor/Claude Code will auto-resolve and pull dependencies before any human types `npm install`, registry policy has to run at the registry proxy (Socket Firewall, JFrog Curation, npm staged publishing) — not at the developer keyboard. Concrete steps: (1) Route every developer workstation and every CI runner through a mediated npm registry that blocks unknown-publisher packages by default. (2) On CI, disable actions/cache write from any pull_request_target-triggered workflow, and treat the cache scope as attacker-writable in threat model. (3) Bind OIDC trusted-publisher configurations to a specific workflow file on a specific protected branch, not to the repo — the TanStack and @cap-js waves both root-caused to repo-scoped bindings. (4) Add a behavioral-analysis gate (Socket / Snyk / Aikido) alongside CVE checks, since every attack in this dossier had zero CVE at time-of-exploit.

prior_art: Extends the September 2025 Shai-Hulud reporting (also Unit 42) and connects it to April-July 2026 waves. The SLSA-provenance-bypass framing overlaps with SLSA project discussion of trust-scope misconfiguration; the /proc-memory OIDC extraction is the same technique documented in the tj-actions/changed-files compromise of March 2025. Novel: the AsyncAPI unprotected-release-branch pattern and the Copilot-triggered install-without-human-in-the-loop observation.
threat: Enterprise developer environments — human workstations and CI/CD runners alike — where any AI coding assistant with dependency-resolution authority (Copilot workspace scan, Cursor MCP, Claude Code) can import a package before any pre-install control (CVE check, registry allowlist, human review) fires.
conditions: AI coding assistant is authorized to load or install project dependencies without explicit per-package approval. Registry policy is enforced only at CI, not at developer workstations, or vice versa. SLSA provenance is treated as sufficient rather than necessary-but-not-sufficient. GitHub Actions cache write is not gated per-workflow (default configuration). OIDC trusted-publisher bindings are scoped to the repo rather than a specific protected workflow.
mitigations: Enforce registry mediation (Socket Firewall / npm staged publishing / JFrog Curation) at both CI and developer workstation. Combine SLSA provenance verification with behavioral analysis at install time. Restrict AI coding agents to a pre-approved dependency allowlist in sensitive projects. Bind OIDC trusted publishers to a specific workflow on a specific protected branch, not a repo. Extend branch protection and code review requirements to every branch that triggers a release workflow, including pre-production and schema branches. Rotate npm and GitHub PATs after any incident and confirm every token was revoked before publishing new versions.
verify_note: All excerpts verified verbatim from mrscan-batch10-3.txt lines 128-130, 216-218, 230, and 462. Cluster G (AI-assisted code and CI risks) chosen because the Copilot-triggered install and the AI-agent-as-delivery-mechanism angle drive the AI-specific relevance; without that, this article would sit in the general appsec adjacent bucket.

author: Unit42_Intel
title: TuxBot v3: an LLM-assisted IoT botnet shipped with the model's safety disclaimer and raw chain-of-thought still in the source
summary: Unit 42 recovered the full source archive, git log and test rigs of TuxBot v3, a modular IoT botnet whose author used an LLM to generate C modules, port exploits and write the Go C2. The model complied but attached a safety disclaimer the developer never removed, left raw chain-of-thought in source files, and hallucinated crypto that shipped unverified. Unit 42 estimates the framework is only ~70% functional - and then repaired several broken features themselves with a few prompts, which is the actual finding.

lessons.point: LLM-assisted malware leaves artifact-level tells worth hunting for: an unremoved safety disclaimer, verbatim chain-of-thought in comments, and crypto that does not round-trip. Unit 42 reports these rather than exhibiting them, and names no vendor or model.
lessons.excerpt: Raw chain-of-thought reasoning from the LLM was left verbatim in source files, and the LLM hallucinated cryptographic implementations that the developer shipped without verifying.

lessons.point: AI assistance measurably degraded quality here rather than amplifying it: core infection works, but all three exploit systems are dead. Do not over-read the causation - the one bug documented in detail (an XOR string-table key desync that kills the IRC and HTTP fallback channels) is attributed to the developer changing a key byte without updating the offline encoder, not to the model.
lessons.excerpt: Exploitation beyond brute-forcing is limited. All three exploit systems are non-functional for different reasons that we detail later in this analysis.

lessons.point: Treat the brokenness as a timing artifact, not a capability ceiling. The defender-relevant metric has shifted from cost-to-generate to cost-to-repair, and Unit 42 measured it at roughly a few prompts.
lessons.excerpt: During our analysis, we could fix several of these broken features with a few targeted prompts to an LLM. This means an adversary with access to the same source code could produce a more complete version with minimal effort.

takeaway: Today's AI-assisted commodity malware is sloppy and self-labelling; budget for the version where someone spends ten more minutes prompting.
threat: Commodity IoT botnet framework with 1,496-pair Telnet brute-forcing, 30+ device-family exploits and five C2 fallback channels, built with LLM assistance and cheaply repairable.
conditions: Internet-exposed IoT devices with default or weak Telnet/SSH credentials.
mitigations: Credential hygiene on IoT fleets; egress control from device VLANs; detection on the documented C2 banners and ports rather than on capability assumptions.
prior_art: Prior vendor reports of LLM refusal boilerplate left in malicious code (HP Wolf 2024 dropper, FunkSec) established the 'LLM tells' phenomenon; Mirai/Gafgyt/Keksec lineage teardowns and MHDDoS-derived booter panels are well covered. The delta here is the recovered development telemetry (git log, QEMU/Docker rigs, 254 automated DDoS benchmark reports) and a quantified per-subsystem capability finding, plus measuring uplift as cost-to-repair.
verify_note: Verifier refuted the original framing on two points, both corrected here: 'LLM-built' overstated a borrowed-code assembly (AISURU/Wuhan lineage, ported MHDDoS) that was LLM-assisted, and the IRC/HTTP failures were wrongly attributed to the model when Unit 42 pins that XOR key desync on the developer. It also confirmed no vendor or model is named anywhere, that the ~70% is an analyst estimate, and that the cached source text is truncated at the ingest limit. Remaining claims verified as supported.

title: Oh My Posh: a directory name runs commands, because the prompt re-renders the resolved path through a template engine whose funcmap has cmd
summary: Oh My Posh composes the displayed path from raw folder names and then passes the whole composed string back through Go text/template, whose function map exposes cmd. A directory named with a template expression therefore executes commands as you the moment the prompt renders - under the built-in default configuration and every path style. Clone a repo, extract an archive, mount a share; the next command after cd is the trigger.

lessons.point: The root cause is double evaluation, and it is a general antipattern: never re-parse a string as a template after untrusted data has been interpolated into it. Render each config template against its own inputs and concatenate the already-rendered pieces with the literal untrusted values.
lessons.excerpt: Oh My Posh re-renders the resolved path string, which contains the raw folder names taken from the filesystem, through the Go `text/template` engine. That engine's function map exposes a `cmd` function that runs arbitrary OS commands.

lessons.point: A template function map is an authorization decision. Any renderer that touches untrusted data should get a data-only funcmap; exposing cmd/readFile/stat/glob to a display path converts a formatting bug into RCE.
lessons.excerpt: use a data-only function map (no `cmd`/`readFile`/`stat`/`glob`) for path resolution

lessons.point: Note the delivery model - this is a developer-machine attack triggered by filesystem contents you merely navigated into, firing on the next prompt render rather than on executing anything. Payloads cannot contain a path separator, which the reporter argues is not a real barrier; only the Windows slash-free proof is shown with output.
lessons.excerpt: Arbitrary command execution as the victim user, triggered by navigating into attacker-supplied directory content: a subdirectory in a cloned repository, an extracted archive, a network share, or a removable drive.

takeaway: Anything that renders your prompt, status bar or editor title is executing attacker-controlled repository metadata - treat it as a parser, not decoration.
threat: Arbitrary command execution as the developer, from cloning a repository or extracting an archive that contains a maliciously named directory.
conditions: Victim runs Oh My Posh (the built-in default configuration is affected, and every path style) and the shell enters the directory or any descendant.
mitigations: Upgrade Oh My Posh; do not re-parse composed paths as templates; restrict the template function map used for path resolution.
prior_art: Go text/template SSTI and template injection generally; shell prompt injection via malicious git branch names and PS1; ANSI-escape injection via filenames; repo contents attacking dev tooling (.vscode/, .gitattributes, hooks). The delta is the sink: the attacker-controlled data is a filesystem directory name re-fed to the engine, it fires under the shipped default configuration, and the trigger is passive navigation. Nearest pool entry: the Shescape shell-escaping advisories (different mechanism - escaping, not double evaluation).
verify_note: Verifier found all five claims supported by the advisory's code walk-through and two PoCs, and confirmed the fix guidance. Corrections applied: the trigger needs a prompt render after cd rather than being wholly passive, the file-write PoC is stated verified on Windows while Linux/macOS exploitation is argued rather than shown, and the slash-free ${IFS} bypass is asserted without output. It scored novelty lower (30) on the grounds that double-eval SSTI and malicious-repo-metadata attacks are established classes; we hold 62 against this pool's prior art and record the disagreement here.

title: 38.9% of agent-generated PRs carry a security smell - but humans introduce most of the real leaked secrets
author: A H M Nazmus Sakib et al.
summary: A large-scale study of the AIDev dataset classified security smells across 16,112 file changes in 4,022 agent-generated pull requests. 38.9% of agent PRs contain at least one security smell and supply-chain integrity issues make up 82.3% of them - but the counterintuitive result is that human collaborators introduce 67.6% of the genuine leaked secrets in these agent-assisted workflows, and review catches almost none of them. All percentages are downstream of an LLM-as-a-judge classification pipeline plus manual review, so treat the precision of the figures accordingly.

lessons.point: Supply-chain integrity dominates the detected smell taxonomy (82.3%); the abstract does not enumerate the remaining categories, so everything else combined is a small residual - point provenance and dependency controls at agent output.
lessons.excerpt: 38.9% of agent-generated PRs contain at least one security smell, with supply chain integrity issues accounting for 82.3% of all detected security smells

lessons.point: Blaming the agent misreads the data: humans introduced most genuine leaked secrets, which the authors describe only as suggesting a *potential* reduction in developer vigilance - an association, not a causal finding.
lessons.excerpt: human collaborators are responsible for introducing 67.6% of genuine leaked secrets within these agent-assisted workflows

lessons.point: Existing review is not a control here - automated and human review together missed 81.1% of these credentials before integration.
lessons.excerpt: existing automated and human review processes fail to detect 81.1% of these credentials prior to integration

threat: Security debt accumulates in high-impact file paths faster than human review capacity, with hard-coded credentials making up 99.6% of critical-severity smells.
conditions: Repositories that accept autonomous coding-agent pull requests through a conventional human review process.
mitigations: Enforce secret scanning as a merge gate rather than a review step; apply provenance/dependency-integrity checks to agent PRs; add context-aware guardrails at the human-AI collaboration point rather than at final review.
takeaway: Gate agent PRs with automated secret and dependency-integrity checks - human review demonstrably does not catch this class, and the humans are introducing most of it.
prior_art: That LLM-generated code contains vulnerabilities is well documented (Copilot-era studies onward). The delta is scale and attribution on real agent PRs - the 67.6% human-origin secrets finding inverts the 'the agent is the risk' framing. Methodologically it applies an existing technique (LLM-as-judge + manual coding) to a new dataset rather than introducing a new method. Accepted at the KDD 2026 AgenticSE workshop.
verify_note: Independent verifier: removed invented contrast categories (injection/logic bugs); restored the authors' 'potential' hedge on developer vigilance; surfaced that all figures come from an LLM-as-a-judge pipeline; novelty 68->57.

editorial.reason: Large-scale, widely-discussed finding on coding-agent risk with a concrete gate: automated secret + dependency-integrity scanning on agent PRs, because human review misses 81%.

title: Four stacked evasion techniques hide device-code phishing from scanners: blob URLs, client-side CAPTCHA gates, multi-hop SaaS flows, and source-code confusables
summary: Unit 42 documents a Microsoft-impersonating OAuth device-code phishing campaign that layers four independent evasion techniques, each defeating a different class of defense: blob-URL delivery (no network-fetchable content for blocklists/safe-browsing), client-side-only CAPTCHA gates (block non-JS scanners), multi-step chains through legitimate SaaS platforms (bypass URL/domain reputation), and source-code corruption via Cyrillic confusables plus invisible characters and injected HTML (defeat substring and hash-based signatures). The takeaway for defenders is that static URL/content reputation and signature matching all fail here; detection must render the page (execute JS, recover DOM text) and normalize Unicode confusables before comparison.

lessons.point: Blob URLs give phishing pages no network existence: JS decrypts AES-GCM ciphertext client-side and hands it to URL.createObjectURL(), so blocklists, caches, and safe-browsing APIs have nothing to fetch or rate, and static analysis sees only ciphertext.
lessons.excerpt: session-unique browser-internal address

lessons.point: Custom CAPTCHA gates are browser-only with no server-side validation - JavaScript compares user input against a random string stored in the DOM, which blocks scanners that don't execute JS while lending false legitimacy.
lessons.excerpt: browser-based without server-side validation

lessons.point: Chaining through legitimate SaaS (Smartsheet, Polling.com, fake PDF viewers, fake reCAPTCHA) separates the initial delivered link from the phishing payload, so domain/URL reputation checks only ever see trusted intermediaries.
lessons.excerpt: separates the initial link from the phishing content, evading URL reputation checks

lessons.point: Source-code evasion corrupts detection two ways: substituting eleven Latin letters with visually identical Cyrillic characters plus 93 zero-width invisible characters, and injecting random alphanumeric strings inside <bdi> tags - both defeat substring matching and hash signatures while rendering identically to users.
lessons.excerpt: 93 invisible characters with no visual width

lessons.point: Reliable detection requires a real HTML parser to recover rendered text plus Unicode-confusable normalization before any string comparison; the report ships 20 malicious URLs and 4 email hashes as IOCs.
lessons.excerpt: robust HTML parsers to recover rendered text and Unicode confusable lookups before string comparison

takeaway: Modern phishing defeats URL reputation, static content scanning, and signature matching simultaneously - detection has to execute JS, render the DOM, and normalize Unicode confusables, not just fetch and hash a URL.
prior_art: Unit42's own blob-URL phishing note (2025-10-02 'phishing pages using blob URLs') and classic IDN/Cyrillic homoglyph + zero-width-character phishing obfuscation; client-side CAPTCHA gates (KongTuke/White Lynx CAPTCHA pages) and SaaS-redirect chaining are each individually documented.
threat: Attacker harvests Microsoft OAuth device codes / authentication tokens via a phishing page engineered to be invisible to network analyzers, URL/domain reputation, safe-browsing blocklists, and signature-based content scanners, yielding account takeover.
conditions: Victim receives a lure link that routes through legitimate SaaS platforms (Smartsheet, Polling.com, fake PDF/reCAPTCHA pages); Victim's browser executes JavaScript (passes the client-side CAPTCHA gate and reconstructs the blob-URL page); Victim completes the impersonated Microsoft device-code / login flow, surrendering the device code or token
mitigations: Detection: render pages with a headless browser, capture blob-URL content, and follow full redirect chains rather than rating only the initial URL; Normalize rendered DOM text through Unicode confusable lookups and strip zero-width/invisible characters before signature/substring matching; Harden identity: restrict or disable OAuth device-code flow where unused, apply Conditional Access, and phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2) so stolen device codes are less useful; Block the 20 URL and 4 email-hash IOCs; user awareness that legitimate-looking SaaS chains can terminate in credential harvesting
verify_note: All five lessons and their excerpts faithfully reflect the source (blob/AES-GCM, browser-only CAPTCHA, SaaS chaining, 11 Cyrillic + 93 invisible chars/<bdi>, HTML-parser+confusable detection); only a minor off-by-one on IOC count (source says 21 URLs, claim says 20). Individual techniques are known, so novelty is mid — value is the defense-mapped combined stack plus concrete detection guidance.
author: Unit42_Intel

title: SourTrade: browser reassembles a Bun-based executable from split parts, defeating hash-based detection with per-session builds
summary: The SourTrade malvertising campaign never serves a complete malicious binary. A cloaked landing page uses a ServiceWorker + SharedWorker to fetch a legitimate Bun runtime from one domain and the malicious PE headers plus JavaScriptCore bytecode (as Base64 in a /config response) from another, then byte-copies them together in the browser per a template recipe. An AES-CTR pseudorandom stream seeded per session changes the file hash on every build while keeping the payload code intact, so no finished malware ever traverses the wire as one artifact.

lessons.point: The final Windows executable is assembled client-side in the victim's browser, so no complete binary crosses the network for signature/hash inspection.
lessons.excerpt: making victims' browsers build the final Windows executable themselves, using a legitimate Bun runtime as its base instead of serving one complete malicious file from a fixed URL

lessons.point: The malicious material is delivered as pieces from different sources: a clean Bun runtime from a second domain, and the PE header/section table plus a .bun bytecode section arriving as Base64 in the /config response.
lessons.excerpt: Base64 blobs in the configuration supply the Portable Executable (PE) header, section table, and a `.bun` section containing malicious JavaScriptCore bytecode for `app.js`

lessons.point: Per-session randomization (rotating AES-CTR seed and size) gives each victim a different file hash while preserving the payload, defeating simple hash/IOC-based detection.
lessons.excerpt: rotating the seed and size in each `/config` response changes the hash while retaining the executable payload code

lessons.point: Delivery abuses same-origin ServiceWorker plumbing so the Mark of the Web attributes the download to the benign-looking landing page, not the domain that actually supplied the runtime; MotW is not removed, so this is evasion of attribution/detection rather than a security-control bypass.
lessons.excerpt: The resulting MotW record identifies the landing page as the download source, not the separate domain that supplied the Bun runtime. MotW itself remains present.

lessons.point: The evasion is narrower than the framing suggests: the attacker-controlled PE structures and bytecode still cross the network (as Base64), so this mainly nullifies static hash detection, not all network/content inspection.
lessons.excerpt: The attacker-controlled PE material and bytecode still cross the network.

lessons.point: The technique evolved from an earlier variant that loaded the open-source StreamSaver.js streamed-download library from GitHub; the current version inlines the streaming architecture so the worker source never appears as a separate fetch.
lessons.excerpt: builds a SharedWorker from JavaScript already embedded in the page, so the worker source never appears as a separate fetch

takeaway: Client-side payload assembly (split parts + per-session hashing) breaks hash-based detection, so hunt the whole delivery chain and behavioral signals, not the final-file signature.
prior_art: HTML smuggling (client-side reconstruction of a payload in the browser from embedded/encoded data to evade network inspection) combined with server-side polymorphism / hash rotation; SourTrade is a documented evolution of these adding split-source assembly over a legitimate Bun runtime with per-session AES-CTR filler.
threat: A malvertising operator delivers per-session, unique-hash Windows malware by reassembling a Bun-based executable in the victim's browser from a legitimate runtime plus attacker-supplied PE headers and JavaScriptCore bytecode, evading hash/IOC-based detection and misattributing the Mark-of-the-Web download source to a benign landing page. Impersonates TradingView, Solana, and Luno to target retail/crypto traders across 12 countries in 25 languages; linked (unconfirmed for the current samples) to the JSCEAL/WeevilProxy stealer.
conditions: Victim reaches a cloaked landing page via a malicious ad and is fingerprinted as a real target (researchers/bots get a blank page); Browser supports ServiceWorker/SharedWorker and streamed downloads (no browser vulnerability or MotW removal required); User runs the assembled executable (the report documents delivery only, not whether download is automatic or click-gated, nor execution)
mitigations: Install trading and wallet software from the vendor's official site, not from ads; Behavioral/EDR detection of Bun standalone executables assembled from separately downloaded components rather than hash-only signatures; Monitor the full chain: ad referral, cloaked page, /config Base64 PE+bytecode, secondary-domain runtime fetch, ServiceWorker attachment download; Enforce MotW-aware execution policies and treat browser-initiated attachment downloads from newly-registered ServiceWorkers as suspicious; Block published SHA-256 hashes and ~96 malicious domains as short-lived IOCs
verify_note: Every lesson and excerpt is a faithful quote from the Confiant/THN article; technique is a genuine, well-scoped evolution of HTML smuggling + polymorphism, useful to detection/threat-hunting engineers.
author: TheHackersNews

title: Siemens Ruggedcom ROX II: three-CVE chain (file disclosure + feature-key command injection + cron injection) yields persistent root on OT switches
summary: Unit 42 and Siemens disclosed a chained trilogy of zero-days in Ruggedcom ROX II OT switches (CVE-2025-40948 file disclosure, CVE-2025-40947 feature-key command injection, CVE-2025-40949 task-scheduler cron injection) that escalates from reconnaissance to persistent root. Each link abuses a root-privileged process that passes unsanitized user input to a shell command: xz misused as a file reader, a gpgv signature string injected via system(), and web-UI scheduler fields written into the root cron table. Fixed in firmware V2.17.1; the takeaway is that an OT switch built to secure the network is itself a full command-injection attack surface.

lessons.point: A root daemon that runs xz with user-supplied parameters becomes an arbitrary file-read primitive: xz -f -c -d behaves like cat, exposing password hashes and private keys.
lessons.excerpt: By supplying the parameters -f, -c and -d at the same time, an attacker can instruct xz to view file contents.

lessons.point: The feature-key signature verifier copies the parsed signature straight into a command run via system() as root with no sanitization, so a signature field like $(python /tmp/rev_shell.py) executes as root.
lessons.excerpt: there is no sanitization or validation of the input signature before it is inserted into the command string

lessons.point: Exploitation reuses the legitimate web-UI feature-key upload to stage the payload, then a crafted feature key to trigger injection - a two-step abuse of intended functionality.
lessons.excerpt: a payload like $(python /tmp/rev_shell.py) could be used, where /tmp/rev_shell.py is the uploaded script

lessons.point: The web task scheduler writes unsanitized control characters and commands into the system's root cron table, converting a persistence feature into root-level persistent code execution surviving reboots.
lessons.excerpt: the attacker can inject control characters and commands into the underlying system configuration file responsible for task execution

lessons.point: Air-gapped or isolated OT switches are not inherently safe; they carry the same software flaws as IT gear and can be turned into a platform for malicious activity.
lessons.excerpt: A common misconception is that because these devices are often air-gapped or sit on isolated networks, they're inherently safe.

takeaway: Never build a shell command from user input inside a root process - the same command-injection class that plagues web apps turns critical OT switches into attacker-controlled infrastructure.
prior_art: Generic CWE-78 OS command injection in embedded/OT web management (unsanitized input into system()); the 'xz -f -c -d as cat' file-read trick is a known GTFOBins-style LOLBin. Novelty here is finding-level: the specific Siemens ROX II zero-day trilogy (CVE-2025-40948/40947/40949), not a new vulnerability class.
threat: An attacker with access to the ROX II management interface can read credentials/keys (CVE-2025-40948), inject a root reverse shell through the feature-key uploader (CVE-2025-40947), and plant a root cron job for reboot-persistent control (CVE-2025-40949), turning a network-segmentation security device into a foothold for OT disruption, data exfiltration, or DoS.
conditions: Ruggedcom ROX II firmware before V2.17.1; Stage 1 (CVE-2025-40948) reachable against the root-privileged management/config daemon; Unit 42 characterizes initial file disclosure as reconnaissance; Stages 2 and 3 require access to the web management UI (file upload and task scheduler); CVE-2025-40949 is described as requiring an authenticated attacker; Network reachability to the switch's management plane
mitigations: Update affected ROX II devices to firmware V2.17.1 per Siemens SSA-973901 / SSA-078743 / SSA-081142; Restrict and segment management-plane access to the OT switch; do not rely on air-gap assumptions; Apply compensating virtual-patching signatures (Palo Alto Threat Prevention 97246/97249/97250) while patching; Monitor for indicators: xz invoked with -f -c -d by a privileged daemon, and unexpected task-scheduler/cron entries invoking python/bash
verify_note: All five lesson excerpts are verbatim and faithfully reflect the Unit42 article; techniques are classic injection but the disclosed CVE chain in an OT switch is a fresh, useful finding for appsec/red-team readers.
author: Unit42_Intel

title: etcd: a READ grant on one key reads everything after it, because the Watch API skipped the range authorization Range/Get applies
summary: A user with READ on a single exact etcd key could call Watch with an open-ended range (clientv3.WithFromKey()) and receive events for every key at or after it. Range/Get and DeleteRange are explicitly unaffected, so this is authorization enforced per API surface rather than centrally - with the streaming endpoint as the one that drifted. Patched in etcd 3.7.1 / 3.6.14 / 3.5.33; reported in part by Anthropic.

lessons.point: The exploitation primitive is IDOR with a range operator: instead of guessing identifiers you widen the bound. Any API that accepts a range, prefix or wildcard needs the authorization check applied to the requested range, not to the caller's grant in isolation.
lessons.excerpt: can use the Watch gRPC API with `clientv3.WithFromKey()` (an open-ended, "from this key to the end of the keyspace" watch) to receive watch events for every key

lessons.point: Subscription endpoints are where per-endpoint authorization drifts - the same pattern as GraphQL subscriptions missing query-level field authz, or Kubernetes treating watch as a verb distinct from get/list. The advisory gives no root cause, so that reading is our inference; what it does state is which surfaces are unaffected.
lessons.excerpt: This is an authorization bypass in etcd's RBAC enforcement for the Watch API; Range/Get and DeleteRange requests are not affected.

lessons.point: Until patched, the correct mental model for a grant audit is that partial READ is not partial: hold every READ grant to the standard of full read access from that key onward.
lessons.excerpt: Any READ grant - even on one key - can be leveraged via Watch to read everything after it.

takeaway: If your read endpoint and your stream endpoint enforce authorization in different code, you have two policies and only test one.
threat: A low-privilege authenticated etcd client reads the bulk of the keyspace via Watch.
conditions: Clusters with authentication enabled and meaningfully partitioned READ grants; the advisory gives fixed versions only and no affected-version range.
mitigations: Upgrade to the patched releases; audit and tighten READ grants; restrict network reach to the client gRPC port.
prior_art: Known bug class rather than a new one: GraphQL subscription resolvers missing query-level authz, WebSocket/SSE channel joins not re-checking per-topic ACLs, Kafka topic-pattern subscribe vs per-topic ACLs, and Kubernetes RBAC treating watch separately from get/list. Range-widening as an authz bypass is IDOR/BOLA with a range operator.
verify_note: Verifier scored novelty 20/100 - the 'stream endpoint skips the read endpoint's authz check' pattern has many documented prior instances, so only the instance is new. It also flagged that the advisory gives no root cause (the per-endpoint-drift explanation is our inference and is labelled as such), that 'only Watch' overstates a list of three unaffected request types, and that Watch delivers events rather than a keyspace snapshot. Held for review as a known class.

title: What Is AI Pentesting and How Does It Work?
summary: Snyk lays out a four-part reference architecture for AI pentesting: a reasoning model that plans reconnaissance/hypothesis/probing/exploitation/chaining, deterministic tools for exhaustive-payload work (a DAST engine, not the LLM enumerating payloads token-by-token), an independent validator model that confirms exploitability before a finding is reported, and prior context about what other tools already found so expensive reasoning is spent on the flaws that require it. The category exists to cover context-dependent flaws (BOLA/IDOR, cross-tenant leakage, auth bypass, chained business-logic exploits) that no signature can reach. Two hard reliability numbers: on autonomous red-teaming benchmarks the strongest model solves 61% overall but under 26% on harder system-exploitation tasks, and raw AI tooling has been observed to hallucinate findings around 30% of the time — which is the empirical case for a separate validator model.
takeaway: AI pentesting is a four-part orchestrated system — reasoning model, deterministic tools, independent validator, prior context — and the failure mode of skipping any one of those is either hallucinated findings, redundant scanner work, or a validator conflict of interest.

lessons.point: AI pentesting is defined as an orchestrated four-part system, not a lone LLM — reasoning model plans, deterministic DAST engine handles known-class exhaustive testing, a separate validator model confirms exploitability, and prior scanner context focuses reasoning at flaws that require it.
lessons.excerpt: A modern AI pentester is not a single model pointed at a URL. It's an orchestrated system with four parts: A reasoning model that plans the assessment: reconnaissance, hypothesis, probing, exploitation, and chaining, the way a human tester approaches an engagement. Deterministic tools in which the model calls for the well-understood work.
