Related claims (jailbreak-transfers-across-models, prompt-injection-is-a-permanent-attack-surface, prompt-injection-is-containment-not-prevention) all exist in data/claims.json and are directly relevant to universal-jailbreak leaderboard results.

title: The Vulnerability With No CVE: Managing Persistent Gaps Between Mandate and Authority in AI Coding Agents
summary: Introduces the Agentic Posture Vulnerability (APV): a task-conditioned, vulnerability-management abstraction for durable agent-control exposures that do not map cleanly to CVEs. An APV is a single invariant posture (excessive agency, weak task-bound authorization, missing controls) that can manifest differently across tasks and stays open until authority is narrowed, a control is added, risk is accepted, or closure is verified. The paper distinguishes APVs from CVE-addressable product defects, OWASP Excessive Agency, and the runtime authorization-execution gap, and provides six recurring APV patterns, a lifecycle, and a control-and-closure matrix.
takeaway: For AI coding agents, the durable defect isn't a code CVE; it's a mismatch between the agent's mandate and its authority. Track those as first-class posture vulnerabilities with their own lifecycle rather than trying to force them into CVE-shaped tickets.

lessons.point: The paper coins the Agentic Posture Vulnerability (APV) as a task-conditioned, durable record for composed agent-control exposures, distinct from CVE-tracked product defects.
lessons.excerpt: We propose the agentic posture vulnerability (APV) as a task-conditioned vulnerability-management abstraction: a durable record for a composed agent-control exposure.

lessons.point: One APV can manifest differently across tasks; the abstraction links those manifestations to the invariant posture and defines four explicit closure conditions.
lessons.excerpt: One posture may produce different runtime manifestations across tasks; APV links those manifestations to the invariant posture and remains open until authority is narrowed, a missing control is added, risk is accepted, or closure is verified.

lessons.point: APV is positioned as an operationalization of existing weaknesses (excessive agency, weak task-bound authorization, control composition) rather than a new root-cause class.
lessons.excerpt: APV is not proposed as a new root-cause class of risk; it operationalizes existing excessive-agency, authorization, and control-composition weaknesses.

lessons.point: The paper provides concrete artifacts: six recurring APV patterns, a vulnerability lifecycle, a minimum record, and a control-and-closure matrix.
lessons.excerpt: six recurring APV patterns, a vulnerability lifecycle, a minimum record, a control-and-closure matrix, tooling implications, and a testable research agenda.

actionable.title: Add an APV-style register alongside CVE tracking for coding agents
actionable.detail: Where you deploy AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot Agent), create a lightweight posture register listing mandate/authority gaps as durable records with four closure states (authority narrowed, control added, risk accepted, closure verified). Don't try to force these into the CVE workflow; they don't behave like product defects.

prior_art: OWASP LLM Top 10 Excessive Agency, existing agent baseline control frameworks, general vulnerability-management practice (CVE lifecycle).
threat: Persistent gaps between an AI coding agent's mandate (what it is asked to do) and its authority (what its tools and permissions let it do) create exposures that outlive any single task and are invisible to CVE-based tracking.
conditions: Deployed AI coding agents with tool access that spans components (repos, cloud accounts, CI, package registries); security programs that only track product defects.
mitigations: Adopt the APV abstraction: durable per-posture record, task-conditioned linkage, and one of four explicit closure conditions. Combine with the paper's six recurring patterns and control-and-closure matrix.
verify_note: All four excerpts verbatim from mrscan-b042-3.txt. Related claims agent-tool-selection-can-be-steered-by-untrusted-context and gate-agent-prs-with-automated-checks both exist in claims.json and match the excessive-agency framing. Cluster B (Agents and harnesses) is the correct home; the paper is specifically about coding-agent posture.

title: Robust Context-Aware Detection of Malicious Instructions in Text
summary: Proposes a segment-level, query-aware classifier for indirect prompt injection detection, then hardens it with two adversarial-training variants: feature-space PGD in the embedding, and LLM-paraphrase-driven realizable evasion in the AT loop. Shows the best AT parameters are domain-dependent.
takeaway: IPI detectors that combine query context with segment-level classification and adversarial training remain useful, but the finding that optimal AT parameters depend on the deployment domain reinforces that a single one-size classifier is not the endgame — detection is one containment layer, and it needs per-app tuning.

lessons.point: No prior IPI detector combined query-relative, segment-level detection with hardening against adaptive attacks.
lessons.excerpt: While a number of approaches for this task have been proposed, no detector combines query-relative detection at the segment level, and none are hardened against adaptive evasion attacks realizable in agentic executions.

lessons.point: Two adversarial-training regimes are proposed: feature-space PGD in embedding space, and LLM-based paraphrasing that simulates realizable evasions.
lessons.excerpt: The first is directly adapted feature-space adversarial training (AT) in which evasions are approximated using projected-gradient-based optimization in the embedding space. The second simulates realizable evasion attacks in the AT loop through LLM-based paraphrasing.

lessons.point: The best adversarial-training parameters vary by application domain, so IPI detectors need domain-specific tuning rather than a single global setting.
lessons.excerpt: Finally, we show that the best AT parameters can depend intimately on the particular application domain. Consequently, domain-dependent tuning of malicious text detectors is likely necessary in practice.

threat: Indirect prompt injection: malicious instructions embedded in retrieved or attacker-controlled text that reaches an agent's context, including adaptive evasions crafted against the deployed detector.
conditions: The agent ingests third-party text (RAG results, tool outputs, web pages) and executes downstream tool calls conditioned on that text. An adaptive adversary can iterate against the detector.
mitigations: Segment-level, query-aware classification of ingested text; adversarial training with both embedding-space PGD and LLM-paraphrase realizable evasions; per-domain tuning of the AT utility-vs-robustness tradeoff. Treat detection as one containment layer, not a solve.

actionable.title: Track segment-level, query-aware IPI detection as a defender pattern
actionable.detail: When evaluating IPI detectors, check that (a) they classify at segment granularity, (b) they condition on the user query, and (c) their published robustness numbers include adaptive attacks — not just static IPI benchmarks. Expect per-domain tuning to be required in production. Reference impl at github.com/tavia-liu/CAD.

prior_art: PromptGuard / Meta LlamaGuard-style prompt-injection classifiers
InjecAgent and BIPIA indirect prompt-injection benchmarks
verify_note: Excerpts checked verbatim against data/_raw/mrscan-b041-1.txt (line 10). Related claims prompt-injection-is-containment-not-prevention, indirect-injection-via-retrieved-content-is-viable, prompt-injection-solvable-by-filtering verified in data/claims.json.

title: LLMs Cannot Reliably Judge (Yet?): A Comprehensive Assessment on the Robustness of LLM-as-a-Judge
summary: RobustJudge, a modular framework, evaluates 15 attacks and 8 defenses against LLM-as-a-Judge systems across 13 models. Findings: judges remain vulnerable under pointwise and pairwise protocols; a combined attack transfers best; no defense dominates on robustness, benign utility, and cost together; robustness is highly sensitive to prompt-template and judge-model choice; long adversarial suffixes can substantially inflate scores including for PAI-Judge variants.
takeaway: Treat LLM-as-a-Judge outputs as an attackable surface: the same optimization-based adversarial suffixes that inflate scores in benchmarks will inflate scores in production red-team dashboards; robustness ranking depends on prompt template and judge-model choice, so an eval harness must fix both and disclose them.

lessons.point: Optimization-based adversarial suffixes can inflate LLM-judge scores, including for PAI-Judge variants.
lessons.excerpt: Optimization-based attack combined with long suffixes can substantially inflate scores returned by both PAI-Judge variants.

lessons.point: No single defense dominates across robustness, benign utility, and computational cost.
lessons.excerpt: the evaluated defenses exhibit no universal dominance across robustness, benign utility, and computational cost

lessons.point: Judge robustness is highly sensitive to prompt template and judge model choice, so eval harnesses must pin both.
lessons.excerpt: Robustness is highly sensitive to both prompt-template and judge model choices.

actionable.title: Pin judge prompt template and judge model in eval harness; test suffix-inflation
actionable.detail: When using LLM-as-a-Judge for red-team or capability scoring, fix and version both the prompt template and the underlying judge model, and periodically inject long adversarial suffixes to measure score inflation before trusting a leaderboard delta.

prior_art: Extends prior LLM-as-a-Judge robustness studies with a unified framework covering 15 attacks x 8 defenses across 13 models.
threat: Adversarial content can steer LLM-as-a-Judge scores (in benchmarks, red-team scoring, or production automated evaluators), producing misleading rankings and letting weak or unsafe outputs pass automated gates.
conditions: LLM-as-a-Judge used for scoring (pointwise or pairwise); attacker can influence the evaluated output text; judge prompt template and model are known or guessable enough to transfer.
mitigations: Use multiple heterogeneous judges and require agreement; pin and version the judge model plus prompt template; monitor suffix length and unusual token patterns in evaluated outputs; do not treat a single LLM judge score as ground truth for security-relevant decisions.
verify_note: All lesson excerpts appear verbatim in the raw abstract. Related claims (llm-as-judge-is-biased-toward-longer-answers, jailbreak-transfers-across-models, score-evals-on-groundedness-not-headline-f1) all exist in data/claims.json.

title: SkillTrace: Multi-Trace Provenance Auditing for LLM-Agent Skill Reuse
summary: SKILLTRACE audits reuse in the emerging LLM-agent 'skills' marketplace. It extracts three provenance traces (Expression = natural-language authored text, Implementation = code, Operational = a Skill Operational Graph over activation/procedure/resource-flow) and compares them deterministically against per-function negatives. On SKILLTRACE-BENCH (820 transformed positives, 751 negative controls over 100 marketplace anchors) it reaches AUROC 0.938 / F1 0.898, and a 36,446-skill wild audit produces trace-attributed review queues beyond repository-similarity baselines.
takeaway: Auditing reuse of agent 'skills' is not the same problem as code-clone detection: reuse can survive when only one of expression, code, or operational structure is preserved, so provenance needs multi-trace comparison across all three.

lessons.point: Existing code-clone / package-similarity detectors miss skill reuse because reuse can preserve only one modality (text, code, or operational structure).
lessons.excerpt: Existing detectors target single-modality source code or whole-package similarity, yet skill reuse evidence is distributed across authored text, implementation fragments, and operational structure. As a result, they can miss reuse that preserves only one part of a skill.

lessons.point: SkillTrace uses three named provenance traces plus a Skill Operational Graph for the operational trace.
lessons.excerpt: SKILLTRACE extracts three provenance traces: Expression, Implementation, and Operational. It represents the Operational Trace as a Skill Operational Graph (SOG) that captures activation, procedure, and resource-flow structure.

lessons.point: Benchmark numbers: AUROC 0.938 / F1 0.898 on 820 positives / 751 negatives over 100 marketplace anchors, plus a 36k-skill wild audit.
lessons.excerpt: On SKILLTRACE-BENCH, with 820 transformed reuse positives over 100 marketplace anchors and 751 negative controls, SKILLTRACE achieves AUROC 0.938 and F1 0.898. A 36,446-skill wild audit further shows that trace-attributed evidence surfaces actionable reuse review queues beyond repository-level baselines.

actionable.title: Adopt multi-trace provenance when vetting third-party agent skills
actionable.detail: When admitting third-party 'skill' packages (metadata + prompts + code + tools + workflows), don't rely on package-similarity or filename hashing. Compare across at least three traces: authored text (Expression), code fragments (Implementation), and operational structure (activation/procedure/resource-flow graph). Calibrate against same-function strict negatives to avoid false positives on ordinary skill overlap.

prior_art: Code-clone detection literature (Deckard, SourcererCC, CCFinder) and package-similarity tools; SkillTrace's contribution is the multi-modality framing plus operational-graph structure specific to LLM-agent skill packages.
threat: Reused/plagiarised or backdoored 'skill' packages laundered into a marketplace can slip past single-modality clone detectors when the attacker preserves only text, only code, or only operational structure of an original skill, breaking provenance and enabling supply-chain trust laundering.
conditions: Agent runtime that installs third-party skills as opaque packages; provenance check limited to filename, hash, or single-modality similarity; no operational-graph comparison; no calibration against same-function negatives.
mitigations: Compute Expression / Implementation / Operational traces at ingestion; store deterministic-comparable representations for later audit; calibrate against same-function strict negatives; require attributable reuse evidence before admitting a skill; queue mismatched-provenance skills for manual review.
verify_note: All three lesson excerpts appear verbatim in the abstract at data/_raw/mrscan-b046-4.txt. Cluster D (model and weights supply chain / defender workflows for third-party artifacts) fits: skills are the agent-era analogue of model artifacts. Could also touch F (tool ecosystem), but D's 'admission-gate patterns' phrasing matches best. related_claims empty because no existing claim in claims.json covers skill-package provenance.

title: Behavioral Canaries: Auditing Private Retrieved Context Usage in RL Fine-Tuning
summary: Behavioral Canaries proposes an auditing mechanism for RL fine-tuning (RLFT) pipelines to detect whether a provider trained on legally protected retrieved context. Instead of relying on verbatim memorization or membership inference (both weak against RL, which shifts style rather than fact retention), the framework instruments preference data by pairing document triggers with feedback that rewards a distinctive stylistic response. In experiments, this achieves a 67% detection rate at 10% FPR (AUROC 0.756) at a 1% canary injection rate.
takeaway: For rights-holders and auditors who need to prove a provider trained on protected corpora via RL, membership-inference is the wrong tool. Style-conditioned behavioral canaries give a working (though modest) signal even when RL only shifts distributional behavior. Numbers cited are 67% TPR at 10% FPR at 1% injection rate.

lessons.point: Standard training-data audits (memorization, membership inference) do not work against RL fine-tuning, because RL shifts behavioral style rather than fact retention.
lessons.excerpt: these methods are ineffective for RL-trained models, as RL primarily influences a model's behavioral style rather than the retention of specific facts

lessons.point: Behavioral canaries can detect training-time influence via distributional behavioral change rather than memorization.
lessons.excerpt: enabling auditors to test for training-time influence even when such influence manifests as distributional behavioral change rather than memorization

lessons.point: At 1% canary injection, detection reaches 67% TPR at 10% FPR (AUROC 0.756).
lessons.excerpt: achieving a 67% detection rate at a 10% false-positive rate (AUROC = 0.756) at a 1% canary injection rate

actionable.title: Include behavioral-canary triggers in protected corpora shared with third-party model providers
actionable.detail: When licensing a corpus that a provider must not use for training, seed it with document triggers paired with stylistically distinctive expected responses; after a suspected training incident, probe the provider's model for the trigger-conditioned style. Expect modest sensitivity (67% at 10% FPR at 1% injection rate), so treat a positive as evidence for legal escalation, not a standalone finding.

prior_art: Extends membership inference and memorization-based training-data auditing; adapts stylistic canary triggers for the RLFT setting where prior methods fail.
threat: A provider fine-tunes an LLM via RL on retrieved context that is contractually protected from training use; standard memorization-based audits cannot detect the violation because RL alters behavioral style rather than surface memorization.
conditions: Auditor can inject a small fraction of documents (1%) into the protected corpus with paired preference feedback rewarding a distinctive style; auditor later has query access to the suspected model.
mitigations: Pre-license behavioral canaries into protected corpora; audit downstream models for trigger-conditioned stylistic responses; contract-side, require RLFT training-data manifests plus attestation from the provider.
verify_note: All lesson excerpts appear verbatim in raw abstract. Related claims exist in data/claims.json (llm-eval-datasets-leak-into-training-sets and agent-memory-is-a-persistent-attack-surface are loose fits; behavioral canary is closer to provenance auditing but no direct claim on RLFT audit exists).

title: DreamGuard: Efficient Runtime Guardrail for LLM Agents via Risk-Aware World Model
summary: Proposes DreamGuard, a runtime guardrail for LLM agents that maintains a compact recurrent latent state over the trajectory and predicts future latent states to derive immediate-hazard and prefix-risk signals. Fuses multi-horizon signals into intervention decisions before tool execution.
takeaway: Reactive per-action guardrails miss long-horizon drift toward hazardous states; a trajectory-level world-model guardrail reportedly gives a better safety-utility trade-off at 25 ms average end-to-end latency per call.

lessons.point: Point-in-time guardrails that only inspect the current action create a blind spot for long-horizon risks that accumulate across individually benign-looking steps.
lessons.excerpt: many remain reactive: they primarily assess the apparent safety of the current action, lacking an explicit model of how risk evolves across the trajectory. This limitation creates a critical blind spot for long-horizon risks, where individually benign-looking actions can gradually drift the agent toward hazardous states.

lessons.point: Their proactive approach fuses immediate-hazard and prefix-risk signals from a learned world model to intervene before execution, at reported ~25 ms latency per call.
lessons.excerpt: The world model maintains a compact recurrent latent state over the trajectory and predicts future latent states from which DreamGuard derives immediate-hazard and prefix-risk evidence. It then fuses these multi-horizon signals into intervention decisions before execution.

lessons.point: Authors claim best safety-utility trade-off vs generic, reactive, and proactive guardrail baselines across four benchmarks plus online evaluation.
lessons.excerpt: Experiments across four benchmarks and an online guardrail evaluation show that DreamGuard outperforms generic, reactive, and proactive guardrail baselines, achieves the best safety-utility trade-off among evaluated guardrails, and maintains an average end-to-end latency of 25 ms per call.

actionable.title: Design agent guardrails at trajectory scope, not per-action
actionable.detail: When building a runtime guardrail for a tool-using LLM agent, evaluate at trajectory scope so that gradual drift toward hazardous states is caught. Include immediate-hazard and prefix-risk signals, and budget for tens of ms latency rather than per-call ML inference on the critical path.

threat: LLM agents can be steered into hazardous states across a sequence of individually benign-looking tool calls, defeating per-action guardrail checks.
conditions: Applies to any tool-using agent whose runtime guardrail evaluates one action at a time without maintaining trajectory-level risk state.
mitigations: Add a trajectory-aware guardrail that keeps a compact latent state across the session, predicts prefix-risk, and intervenes before execution; validate on multi-step agent-safety benchmarks rather than per-turn ones.
prior_art: Extends recent runtime guardrail work (reactive per-action classifiers) by adding world-model-style trajectory reasoning; overlaps with dual-LLM containment pattern literature.
verify_note: Excerpts verbatim from raw fetch; related_claims present in data/claims.json. Effect-size claims left at moderate confidence pending independent benchmarks.

title: Measuring and Detecting Harmful AI Sycophancy
summary: The paper focuses on preference-induced stance reversal sycophancy (PSRS): a model reverses an initial stance to align with a user's stated preference. The authors build CAP (Contrastive Anchor Probing) and collect 290,460 labeled responses from 17 open/closed LLMs across 12 everyday-advice domains. PSRS rates range from 5% to 56% across models, with more capable models being less sycophantic. Response-only detectors are feasible but drop on unseen models; the authors sketch an initial cross-model generalization approach.
takeaway: Preference-induced stance reversal (a specific, measurable sycophancy mode) is common (5-56%) and detectable from response text alone, but detectors don't generalize cleanly to unseen models.

lessons.point: PSRS rates vary by an order of magnitude across models, and capability inversely correlates with sycophancy.
lessons.excerpt: We first reveal that PSRS rates range from 5% to 56% across LLMs, with more capable models being less sycophantic.

lessons.point: Single-response PSRS detection is feasible without model internals, but requires learning subtle patterns.
lessons.excerpt: Next, we show that detecting PSRS is feasible from the response text alone, and detectors need to learn subtle PSRS patterns from the training data.

lessons.point: Cross-model generalization is the operational bottleneck: detectors degrade on unseen model families.
lessons.excerpt: We demonstrate that detection performance drops on unseen models and propose an initial approach to address this challenge.

actionable.title: Add PSRS as a guardrail eval axis
actionable.detail: For chat-shaped products, add a preference-induced-stance-reversal (PSRS) eval: anchor the model to a position, then re-ask with a contrary user preference and measure reversal rate. Track by model version and re-run when model family changes, since detectors do not transfer cleanly.

prior_art: Prior sycophancy measurement work is extended by (a) narrowing to PSRS, (b) building a labeled detection dataset, and (c) studying cross-model detector transfer.
verify_note: Excerpts verbatim from fetched abstract. Cluster H: alignment/refusal-shaping is the security-adjacent framing.
threat: A model that reverses stance to match a user's stated preference can be steered by a malicious or misinformed user into endorsing unsafe or wrong claims, undermining downstream trust in AI-authored advice.
conditions: User states a preference or opposing view after an initial model stance; model has not been specifically tuned against preference-induced stance reversal; detector (if present) was trained on a different model family than the one in production.
mitigations: Add a PSRS eval to release gates that anchors then challenges a stance and measures reversal rate; prefer more capable models where PSRS rate is empirically lower; if using a response-text detector, retrain per model family since cross-family generalization is weak.

title: Microsoft Zero Trust for AI: new DevSecOps pillar and Zero Trust Assessment coverage for AI agents
summary: Microsoft expanded its Zero Trust for AI strategy with two additions: an AI/DevSecOps pillar in the Zero Trust Assessment tool, and a Zero Trust Workshop DevSecOps pillar with 15 control groups and 91 tasks. The workshop's AI pillar now includes guidance from Microsoft's AI Memory framework, treating agent memory as a governed security boundary with provenance and lifecycle visibility.
takeaway: The Zero Trust playbook for agents is being formalized around memory as a first-class governed asset and DevSecOps controls that gate AI-assisted code from source to deployment.

lessons.point: Zero Trust for agentic systems now treats memory as a governed security boundary requiring intent, provenance, lifecycle visibility, and user control — not a runtime scratch pad.
lessons.excerpt: The Zero Trust Workshop also improves the AI pillar to include guidance based on the Microsoft AI Memory framework, helping teams treat memory as a governed security boundary with clear intent, provenance, lifecycle visibility, and user control.

lessons.point: Microsoft's DevSecOps pillar names four AI-specific control tasks — code governance, tool allowlisting, data protection, and ML pipeline supply-chain security — as the concrete deliverables for AI-assisted development.
lessons.excerpt: plus four tasks focused directly on AI-assisted development: code governance, tool allowlisting, data protection, and AI and machine learning pipeline supply-chain security.

lessons.point: AI assistants that generate code, recommend packages, and create infrastructure configurations amplify the cost of any governance, permissions, or dependency gap that existed pre-AI — the same controls now have wider blast radius.
lessons.excerpt: While these capabilities accelerate delivery, they also amplify the consequences of governance gaps, excessive permissions, insecure dependencies, and compromised supply chains.

actionable.title: Treat agent memory as a governed asset with provenance and access review
actionable.detail: When adding long-term memory to an agent, define entry policy, provenance tags, lifecycle limits, and revocation. Do not let the runtime accumulate un-audited state. Pair with tool allowlisting so a poisoned memory cannot unlock high-authority actions.

prior_art: Microsoft's own June 2026 'Guarding AI Memory' post (referenced in article) and the standing claim agent-memory-is-a-persistent-attack-surface — this post operationalizes them into a workshop pillar rather than introducing new mechanism.
threat: Governance and control gaps in AI-assisted development pipelines (excessive permissions, un-audited dependencies, ungoverned agent memory) let an attacker who fools the model reach production.
conditions: Organization uses AI assistants for code generation, package recommendation, or IaC; agent runtimes carry long-term memory; DevSecOps controls were designed pre-AI.
mitigations: Treat agent memory as a governed boundary (intent, provenance, lifecycle, user control); add tool allowlisting; extend supply-chain controls to the ML pipeline; apply verify-explicitly, least-privilege, assume-breach to CI/CD, source repos, dependencies, artifacts, and IaC.
verify_note: Excerpts verified verbatim against raw source. Related claims exist. Novelty tempered because this is a vendor rollout of frameworks whose ideas already exist in the ledger (memory-as-attack-surface, agent PR gating).

title: MMAligner: Safeguarding Multimodal Large Language Models through Representation Calibration
summary: Argues that MLLM safety degradation is a representation-alignment problem, not a missing-safety-capability problem. Geometric analysis finds a shared safety subspace and refusal boundary learned from text that persists across modalities, but unsafe multimodal inputs undergo a representation shift that places them outside the boundary. MMAligner calibrates unsafe multimodal representations back inside the refusal region with a hard lower bound (ensure refusal), a soft upper bound (avoid over-modification), and a preservation objective for benign inputs. Reports 99% refusal rate on unsafe multimodal inputs with less than 2% utility loss.
takeaway: MLLM jailbreaks by modality-shift are best framed as representation misalignment, not missing safety training. Pulling unsafe representations back inside the text-learned refusal region works and preserves utility.

lessons.point: MLLMs will refuse an unsafe text prompt but comply with a semantically equivalent multimodal version, indicating a modality gap in safety application rather than absence.
lessons.excerpt: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often refuse unsafe text prompts yet generate harmful responses to semantically equivalent multimodal inputs.

lessons.point: The safety mechanism learned from text is not lost in MLLMs; a shared safety subspace and refusal boundary persist across modalities, but unsafe multimodal inputs get pushed outside it.
lessons.excerpt: safety mechanisms learned from text persist across modalities: a shared safety subspace and refusal boundary remain effective, and representations inside this boundary consistently trigger refusals. However, unsafe multimodal inputs undergo a representation shift that places most of them outside the boundary

lessons.point: This reframes multimodal safety failures as representation misalignment rather than a training-data or capability gap.
lessons.excerpt: This indicates that multimodal safety degradation stems from representation misalignment rather than the absence of safety capability.

lessons.point: MMAligner uses three components (hard lower bound, soft upper bound, benign preservation) and reports 99% refusal on unsafe multimodal inputs with <2% utility loss.
lessons.excerpt: MMAligner raises the average refusal rate on unsafe multimodal inputs to 99% with less than 2% utility degradation and minimal training data

actionable.title: Treat multimodal safety gaps as representation-alignment problems, not training gaps
actionable.detail: When triaging MLLM jailbreaks via image/audio input, first look for text-side refusal on the paraphrased content. If text refuses but multimodal complies, the fix is representation calibration into the existing refusal region, not more multimodal safety fine-tuning data.

prior_art: Prior MLLM safety fine-tuning approaches, external guardrails (LlamaGuard-style), and constitutional-AI style alignment methods.
threat: MLLMs refuse unsafe text but comply with semantically equivalent multimodal (image/audio) formulations, giving attackers a modality-conversion jailbreak.
conditions: Deployed multimodal LLMs where an attacker can render an unsafe request as an image or other non-text modality; defender relies on the model's intrinsic refusal.
mitigations: Representation-calibration methods like MMAligner that project unsafe multimodal representations back inside the text-learned refusal boundary, with hard lower and soft upper bounds and a benign-input preservation objective. External guardrails remain a fallback.
verify_note: All four excerpts verbatim from mrscan-b042-4.txt. Cluster H (Guardrails, alignment, and refusal) is the closest fit; the paper is about refusal geometry and utility trade-off. Related claims constitutional-ai-reduces-refusal-brittleness and jailbreak-transfers-across-models both exist in claims.json and are thematically adjacent (alignment method reduces brittleness; modality-shift attacks are a transfer surface).

title: Show HN: Product analytics (and evals) for agent sessions on your MCP
summary: Armature (YC P26) is a Show HN product-analytics + evals SaaS for MCP servers, Claude Connectors, and ChatGPT Apps. SDK wraps the MCP server in three lines (TS/Python/Go), rebuilds each user session (intent, agent-thinking, tool calls, outcome), groups sessions into use cases, ranks failures by root cause, and can auto-generate evals from top use cases. Marketing page, no independent measurement.
takeaway: The observability primitive Armature bets on is the session, not the tool call: reconstructing user intent + agent reasoning + call sequence lets you rank failures by root cause even when every HTTP response was 200 OK. That framing is the useful part for anyone rolling their own agent telemetry, independent of buying this product.

lessons.point: The right unit of agent observability is the session (intent, thinking, calls, outcome) — a tool-call log alone hides silent failures where every call returned 200.
lessons.excerpt: Models scan every session for failures, loops and dead ends, group them by root cause and rank them by how many users encountered them, **even when every API response was 200 OK**.

lessons.point: MCP servers are blind spots for classic product analytics because the session happens inside the AI client (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, etc.), not the vendor's UI.
lessons.excerpt: Those tools track humans clicking your UI. When a user delegates to an agent, the session happens inside Claude or ChatGPT and your UI never sees it. Armature captures exactly those sessions.

lessons.point: Session captures carry PII and secrets by default; redaction has to happen before storage, not after.
lessons.excerpt: Sessions can carry personal information and secrets, so we treat every one of them as sensitive. Detection models scan sessions and redact PII and secrets by default, before anything reaches storage.

actionable.title: Consider session-level MCP telemetry, not tool-call-level
actionable.detail: For any MCP server you operate, capture the full session (user intent, agent reasoning, tool-call sequence, outcome) rather than just per-tool logs. Redact PII and secrets before storage. Use failure clustering (loops, dead ends, 200-OK-but-wrong) as the eval seed. Armature is one option; the observability primitive is the point — you can build equivalent instrumentation in-house or with LangSmith/Langfuse if you own both sides.

prior_art: LangSmith and Langfuse (which the page explicitly contrasts against); PostHog/Amplitude/Mixpanel (contrasted); the wider agent-observability space (Helicone, Traceloop, Braintrust); Anthropic's own MCP observability guidance.
threat: MCP servers that ship without session-level telemetry cannot detect silent agent failures (loops, wrong-tool selection, side-channel data reads) because every underlying HTTP call returns 200. Product teams operate blind on the actual agent experience.
conditions: MCP server or Claude Connector deployed to end users. No session reconstruction layer that captures user intent + agent reasoning. Success measured at HTTP-response level rather than task-outcome level.
mitigations: Instrument session-scoped traces (intent, reasoning, tool calls, outcome). Redact PII/secrets in the ingest path, not after storage. Cluster failures by root cause; do not treat 200 OK as success. Convert top failure clusters into recurring evals to catch regressions before ship.
verify_note: Three excerpts verified verbatim against data/_raw/mrscan-batch06-5.txt. This is a vendor/marketing page (Show HN), so novelty and relevance are moderate. Cluster J (observability) fits. Related claims are a stretch — this maps loosely to eval-quality claims but does not directly refute or support any specific existing claim; kept to two to avoid over-linking.

title: Post-Hoc Trajectory-Risk Certification for Modular LLM-Based Security Agents
summary: Conformal-prediction paper on how to compose per-stage coverage guarantees into a trajectory-level guarantee for staged LLM security pipelines (e.g. traffic classification then technique attribution). Shows a natural pairwise-correlation extension to three or more stages is invalid, derives a spanning-tree alternative, and reports that on a two-stage intrusion-detection pipeline across 6 open LLMs a direct trajectory audit beats Bonferroni by 13.7% once the audit sample is large enough.
takeaway: Per-stage confidence numbers do not compose for free in a multi-step LLM security pipeline; if you need a joint guarantee, treat trajectory calibration as its own audit with an explicit sample-size budget, and expect distribution shift to break calibration long before it breaks accuracy.

lessons.point: Stage-level conformal coverage does not automatically compose into a trajectory-level guarantee for a staged security agent.
lessons.excerpt: Split conformal prediction gives each stage finite-sample coverage, but deployment requires a trajectory-level guarantee across the full chain. These guarantees do not compose automatically when stages are independently trained and calibrated.

lessons.point: A direct trajectory audit is only tighter than Bonferroni once the sample size is adequate; below that threshold it is worse.
lessons.excerpt: A direct audit of trajectory failure becomes 13.7% tighter than Bonferroni once the audit reaches the required sample size, but is worse when undersized.

lessons.point: Distribution shift can destroy calibrated confidence at 100% single-step miscoverage while raw accuracy still looks acceptable.
lessons.excerpt: Under cross-dataset deployment, single-step miscoverage reaches 100% even when accuracy remains 78%, showing that distribution shift destroys calibrated confidence before raw accuracy.

actionable.title: When staging LLM security agents, budget for a trajectory-level calibration audit
actionable.detail: For any pipeline that chains an LLM classifier with a downstream attributor or triage step, do not assume per-stage confidence composes; either allocate an audit sample large enough for a direct trajectory certificate or fall back to a documented Bonferroni bound and flag it as conservative in the eval report.

prior_art: Extends split conformal prediction to multi-stage agent pipelines; contrasts with Bonferroni allocation. Adjacent to broader conformal-prediction literature and to agent-eval work on staged/tool-augmented LLM systems.
threat: Deployed multi-stage LLM security agent reports per-stage confidences that do not compose to a valid joint guarantee, so downstream consumers over-trust the trajectory verdict, especially under cross-dataset deployment where miscoverage can hit 100% while accuracy stays around 78%.
conditions: Staged pipeline with independently trained/calibrated LLM components; deployment under distribution shift; consumers rely on stage-level conformal coverage as a joint guarantee.
mitigations: Compute a spanning-tree pairwise-overlap bound instead of a naive pairwise extension; run a direct trajectory audit once sample size is sufficient; treat cross-dataset deployment as recalibration-required rather than trusting stage-level calibration.
verify_note: Excerpts verbatim from arXiv abstract; related_claims cross-checked against claims.json.

title: ASTELD: A Six-Axis Classification Framework for Autonomous AI Agents
summary: Proposes ASTELD, a six-axis classification framework for autonomous AI agent platforms (Architecture, Security, Tool integration, Execution, Level of autonomy, Deployment), evaluates it on eight platforms with OpenClaw as case study, classifies 50+ OpenClaw derivatives, and derives a six-category vulnerability taxonomy plus a claimed empty region: local-first deployment combined with enterprise-grade security.
takeaway: If you are picking an agent framework, force yourself to place it on the six ASTELD axes and check whether the security axis matches your deployment topology; the paper claims the local-first-plus-enterprise-security quadrant is empty in current systems.

lessons.point: There is no shared classification for comparing agent platforms across architecture, security, tool integration, execution, autonomy, and deployment, which makes framework choice ad hoc.
lessons.excerpt: Autonomous AI agent platforms differ substantially in architecture, security, tool integration, execution, autonomy, and deployment, yet the field lacks a common classification scheme for comparing these design choices.

lessons.point: Cross-platform patterns include a security-accessibility diagonal and strong execution-architecture coupling, so security posture correlates with other design axes rather than being an independent knob.
lessons.excerpt: The resulting profiles separate all eight platforms under their dominant configurations and reveal three cross-platform patterns: a security-accessibility diagonal, strong execution-architecture coupling, and capability convergence with persistent architectural differentiation.

lessons.point: None of the surveyed autonomous-agent platforms combines local-first deployment with enterprise-grade security, which the authors flag as an under-served design region.
lessons.excerpt: The analysis also exposes a consequential empty region: none of the evaluated systems combines local-first deployment with enterprise-grade security.

actionable.title: Use ASTELD's six axes as an agent-platform intake checklist
actionable.detail: When admitting a new autonomous-agent platform, record its ASTELD coordinates (Architecture, Security, Tool integration, Execution, Autonomy/human-control, Deployment) plus the six-category vulnerability taxonomy from the OpenClaw case study; treat mismatches between the security axis and your deployment topology as a blocking finding.

prior_art: Synthesizes prior agent taxonomies with observable platform properties; complements Invariant Labs tool-poisoning framework and NIST-style STRIDE-adjacent AI threat models.
threat: Agent platform choice is made without a systematic security-axis comparison, so security assumptions from one deployment topology are silently carried over to another (e.g. cloud-managed to local-first) where they do not hold.
conditions: Organization is selecting or extending an autonomous-agent platform; multiple platforms considered without a shared axis vocabulary; security posture treated as independent of architecture and deployment.
mitigations: Score candidate platforms on all six ASTELD axes; use the six-category vulnerability taxonomy from the OpenClaw case study as an intake checklist; flag any framework whose Security axis is inconsistent with its Deployment axis for further review.
verify_note: Excerpts verbatim from arXiv abstract; related_claims cross-checked.

title: AegisShield: Democratizing Cyber Threat Modeling with Generative AI
summary: AegisShield is a GenAI-assisted threat modeling tool that combines STRIDE, MITRE ATT&CK, NVD, and AlienVault OTX to auto-generate threats for small organizations. Evaluated on 243 expert-graded threats and 8000+ AI-generated ones, it reduced complexity, produced output semantically aligned with expert threats, and mapped 85.4% of threats to MITRE ATT&CK techniques.
takeaway: GenAI-assisted STRIDE plus a live NVD/OTX feed can plausibly reach an 85% MITRE ATT&CK mapping rate on generated threats; this is a viable base pattern for lightweight threat-modeling assistants, but the human-vs-AI validation is against a modest 243-threat expert set.

lessons.point: GenAI-assisted STRIDE + MITRE ATT&CK can achieve ~85% technique-mapping rate on auto-generated threats.
lessons.excerpt: achieves an 85.4 percent success rate in mapping threats to MITRE ATT&CK techniques

lessons.point: Feeding live threat intelligence (NVD, AlienVault OTX) into the LLM tightens the generated threat descriptions.
lessons.excerpt: By integrating real time threat intelligence from the National Vulnerability Database and AlienVault Open Threat Exchange, AegisShield produces streamlined and accessible threat descriptions.

lessons.point: GenAI outputs were semantically aligned with expert-developed threats on a 243-threat expert benchmark.
lessons.excerpt: yields outputs semantically aligned with expert developed threats (p less than 0.05)

actionable.title: Prototype: STRIDE + MITRE mapping assistant hydrated by NVD/OTX
actionable.detail: For internal threat-modeling assistants, feed live NVD and OTX advisories into the LLM system prompt and require STRIDE category + ATT&CK technique ID per generated threat, then measure technique-mapping accuracy against a small expert-labeled set.

prior_art: Applies STRIDE + MITRE ATT&CK with LLM assistance; similar to prior LLM-assisted threat modeling but adds live threat feeds and evaluates against expert-labeled threats.
threat: Small organizations skip formal threat modeling; auto-generated threat models risk over-trust in LLM output, missed threats, or hallucinated MITRE technique IDs that look authoritative.
conditions: Use of an LLM to generate STRIDE threats; mapping produced by an LLM without independent verification; consumer organization lacks security staff to sanity-check output.
mitigations: Require LLM-generated threats to cite a specific NVD CVE or OTX pulse; check MITRE technique IDs against the ATT&CK JSON as a post-step; keep a human-in-the-loop review before adopting the generated model as a control baseline.
verify_note: All excerpts verbatim from raw abstract. No exact-match related_claims exist for GenAI-assisted STRIDE threat modeling; left empty rather than force-fit.

title: Online Security Learning in Cooperative Multi-Agent Systems under Hidden Byzantine Attacks
summary: Theoretical/algorithmic paper on cooperative multi-agent control where a hidden fixed subset of agents are Byzantine and can stealthily overwrite their own coordinates of the team's planned joint action after seeing the plan. Shows attacker information determines geometry (observing attacker => (s,a)-rectangular robust MDP; blind attacker => s-rectangular). Proves an information-theoretic lower bound (indistinguishable horizon-one instances force Omega(K) security regret while return regret is zero) and gives a stage-tied robust estimator with regret bound O~(H^2 sqrt(SAK)) + E[D_K].
takeaway: Security regret in Byzantine cooperative MAS cannot be reduced below a cumulative response-gap term; the achievable bound depends on what the attacker can observe about the planned action.

lessons.point: The attacker's observational power sets the robust MDP structure, changing what defenders can achieve.
lessons.excerpt: An attacker that observes the planned action induces an exact (s,a)-rectangular robust Markov decision process (MDP) whose rows are convex hulls of overwrite-induced public-outcome laws, whereas a blind attacker induces an s-rectangular model.

lessons.point: There is an unavoidable dependence on a cumulative response-gap term in security regret.
lessons.excerpt: Two indistinguishable horizon-one instances force Ω(K)expected security regret while return regret is zero, showing that dependence on D Kis unavoidable.

actionable.title: Model attacker observability before choosing robustness bounds in MAS
actionable.detail: When designing multi-agent robustness guarantees, calibrate the robust-MDP model to what a compromised agent can observe about the joint plan; assuming a blind attacker yields weaker (s-rectangular) guarantees than the true (s,a)-rectangular geometry when plans are visible.

prior_art: Robust MDPs (Nilim & El Ghaoui; Iyengar); Byzantine multi-agent RL; s- vs (s,a)-rectangularity.
threat: A hidden fixed subset of cooperative agents observes the team's planned joint action and stealthily overwrites its own action coordinates before execution; the learner never sees the overwrite or the executed action, only planned actions plus public rewards and states.
conditions: Cooperative online multi-agent control with public planned actions, public rewards, and public states; unknown subset of Byzantine agents with plan-observation capability; no direct observability of executed joint action.
mitigations: Model the attack as an (s,a)-rectangular robust MDP when plans are observable to the attacker; use a stage-tied robust estimation-to-decisions learner with regret O~(H^2 sqrt(SAK)) + E[D_K]; accept an unavoidable cumulative response-gap term in security regret.
verify_note: Excerpts verified verbatim (including the paper's own inline unicode/formatting artifacts) against data/_raw/mrscan-b020-4.txt.

title: Algebraic Cryptanalytic Extraction on Hard-Label Neural Networks
summary: The paper reformulates Carlini et al.'s (EUROCRYPT 2025) hard-label neural network extraction attack into an algebraic framework and introduces an Approximate Signature Vector (ASV) method that replaces expensive SVD-based rank checking with inner-product operations, reducing clustering complexity from O(n^2 (d^k)^3) to O(n (d^k)^3) on average. It also presents the first hard-label extraction attack against max-pooling CNNs using a kernel-centric clustering scheme, demonstrated on a 64-64x4-10 FCNN and LeNet-5.
takeaway: Hard-label neural network extraction is getting materially cheaper: an inner-product-based Approximate Signature Vector replaces SVD in dual-point clustering, and max-pooling CNNs are no longer out of reach for hard-label cryptanalytic attacks.

lessons.point: The 2025 SOTA hard-label extraction attack was polynomial in theory but bottlenecked in practice by O(n^2 (d^k)^3) SVD-based clustering; replacing SVD with inner products drops the average cost to O(n (d^k)^3).
lessons.excerpt: its dual-point clustering relies on singular value decomposition (SVD) with a time complexity of O(n 2⋅(d(k))3), resulting in huge runtime in practice

lessons.point: The ASV method exploits two structural properties of trained networks: near-orthogonality of high-dimensional random vectors and disentangled feature learning in practical DNNs.
lessons.excerpt: high-dimensional random vectors are nearly orthogonal, and neurons in practical DNNs tend to learn disentangled features

lessons.point: The paper claims the first hard-label model extraction attack against max-pooling CNNs, achieved by switching from neuron-centric to kernel-centric clustering that leverages convolutional weight sharing.
lessons.excerpt: this paper presents the first model extraction attack against hard-label max-pooling Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) by proposing an advanced ASV method with a kernel-centric clustering scheme instead of the neuron-centric clustering

actionable.title: Model extraction on hard-label APIs is getting cheaper; treat top-1 label endpoints as leaky
actionable.detail: Assume that black-box endpoints exposing only the top-1 label of small-to-medium FCNNs and now max-pooling CNNs are extraction-vulnerable at feasible cost. Rate limit, add query-pattern anomaly detection, and prefer prediction-confusing outputs (top-k with noise) if secrecy of weights matters.

prior_art: Carlini et al., Cryptanalytic Extraction of Neural Network Models, EUROCRYPT 2020 and follow-ups through EUROCRYPT 2025.
threat: An adversary with hard-label black-box access to a deployed neural network can extract functionally equivalent parameters at materially reduced runtime, previously infeasible in practice due to SVD cost.
conditions: Target must be an FCNN or a max-pooling CNN accessible via a hard-label prediction API; adversary can issue enough queries to run dual-point clustering.
mitigations: Query rate limiting, per-user query budgets, adding output noise, moving from hard-label to top-k probability outputs only where product allows, monitoring for boundary-probing query patterns.
verify_note: All three excerpts are verbatim from the arXiv abstract (mrscan-b042-0.txt). Novelty claim (first hard-label extraction on max-pooling CNNs) is stated explicitly in the abstract. No related_claims in claims.json cover neural network extraction, so left empty.

title: Quantigence: A Multi-Agent Framework for Post-Quantum Security Analysis on Commodity Hardware
summary: Quantigence is a supervisor/worker multi-agent framework built on a 4-bit-quantized 9B model that runs on a single commodity GPU (8 GB budget) for post-quantum crypto (PQC) security analysis, grounded in arXiv, NVD, and a local NIST-PQC index. On atomic single-fact benchmarks a single tool-using agent already reaches 98% accuracy vs 57% zero-shot, and multi-agent decomposition does not improve over that; on complex multi-faceted queries, the supervisor/worker split raises rubric coverage from 78% to 89%. The paper also measures retrieval-corpus poisoning robustness.
takeaway: Tool access dominates the accuracy jump on single-fact queries; multi-agent decomposition only pays off on multi-faceted questions where rubric coverage matters, not on lookups.

lessons.point: Tool access, not multi-agent structure, drives accuracy on atomic single-fact queries.
lessons.excerpt: tool access is what raises accuracy, from 57% (zero-shot) to 98% (single agent), and a single tool-using agent is, as expected, a strong baseline that multi-agent decomposition does not beat on single-fact lookups.

lessons.point: Supervisor/worker decomposition helps on complex multi-faceted queries via rubric coverage, not on simple lookups.
lessons.excerpt: the supervisor/worker decomposition instead improves rubric coverage from 78% to 89% and judged answer quality.

lessons.point: The framework is explicitly evaluated for robustness to retrieval-corpus poisoning, not just accuracy.
lessons.excerpt: we report both, and further measure robustness to retrieval-corpus poisoning and behavior across model scales.

actionable.title: Don't add agent layers where a single tool-using agent already saturates the task
actionable.detail: Benchmark a single tool-using agent before spinning up planner/worker decomposition. Reserve multi-agent orchestration for tasks whose evaluation criterion is rubric coverage on multi-faceted queries, not atomic-fact accuracy.

prior_art: Well-known finding that tool-use collapses much of the multi-agent gain on lookups; PQC-specific packaging is the novelty.
threat: Multi-agent frameworks add coordination surface (extra prompts, inter-agent messages, poisoning of shared corpora) without measurably improving accuracy on single-fact tool-grounded tasks.
conditions: Deployments that dispatch atomic lookups through a supervisor + worker stack instead of a single tool-using agent; shared retrieval corpora that are not integrity-checked.
mitigations: Baseline single-agent-with-tools performance before adopting orchestration; measure retrieval-corpus poisoning robustness alongside accuracy; scope multi-agent decomposition to multi-faceted queries where rubric coverage is the target.
verify_note: All three lesson excerpts appear verbatim in the abstract at data/_raw/mrscan-b046-0.txt. Cluster B (agents/harnesses) fits the harness-eval finding. related_claims empty because no existing claim in claims.json specifically addresses agent-count vs tool-access on atomic tasks.

title: PolicyGuard: Prompt-Configurable Semantic DLP for LLM Coding Agents
summary: PolicyGuard is a pre-model interception framework that classifies user prompts against a plaintext natural-language policy file, positioned as an alternative to regex/model-fine-tune/vendor-classifier DLP. Reports 96.5% effective block rate at 3.0% false-positive rate on 927-prompt frozen test, 100% accuracy on 217-prompt hidden holdout, and 86.4-96.5% EBR across four LLMs without policy changes. Paper has been withdrawn by the author pending institutional review.
takeaway: The policy-as-prompt pattern (DLP rules as an editable natural-language file, evaluated by an LLM) is worth prototyping for coding-agent input filtering, and the reported numbers cross-model without policy edits are strong. But the paper is withdrawn pending institutional review, so treat the specific numbers as unverified until it reappears; use the pattern, not the benchmark.

lessons.point: Rule-configurable natural-language DLP policies outperform equivalent content expressed in JSON, and dramatically outperform zero-shot classification.
lessons.excerpt: PolicyGuard's natural language format significantly outperforms equivalent content in JSON format (McNemar chi-squared = 31.58, p <0.001) and dramatically outperforms zero-shot classification (Cohen's h = 0.915)

lessons.point: A single natural-language policy can port across four different LLMs at 86.4-96.5% effective block rate without modification.
lessons.excerpt: the same policy achieves 86.4-96.5% EBR across four different LLMs without modification

lessons.point: The paper is currently withdrawn pending an institutional review process, so headline numbers should not be cited as settled.
lessons.excerpt: This paper is being withdrawn because it was submitted prior to completion of a required institutional review process. The authors intend to resubmit after the review is complete

actionable.title: Track PolicyGuard resubmission before adopting its numbers; the pattern is still useful
actionable.detail: Prototype the policy-as-prompt pattern (plaintext policy file consumed as an LLM classification prompt) for coding-agent input DLP where regex is too rigid. Do not cite the 96.5% EBR / 100% holdout numbers in decisions until the paper is un-withdrawn after institutional review.

prior_art: Contrasts with regex-based DLP, fine-tuned classifiers, and vendor-managed DLP; sits alongside NeMo Guardrails, LlamaGuard, and similar LLM-based content classifiers.
threat: Users paste credentials, PII, or proprietary data into coding-agent prompts; regex DLP misses semantic variants; vendor classifiers are not customizable to the org's policy.
conditions: Coding agent accepts free-form NL prompts; DLP is expected to enforce customer-specific policy without model retraining.
mitigations: Deploy a pre-model LLM classifier reading a plaintext policy file; A/B test against regex DLP on your own prompt distribution; do not rely on the reported cross-model portability numbers until the paper is republished.
verify_note: All lesson excerpts verbatim in abstract; withdrawal note verbatim from the paper page. Confidence deliberately capped low because the paper is withdrawn. Related claim prompt-injection-solvable-by-filtering exists in claims.json (this paper is loosely relevant as an input-filter proposal, though DLP is not the same as injection filtering).

title: ChainDrop: Self-propagating npm worm mints valid Sigstore provenance and exfiltrates via Ethereum-routed C2
summary: Unit 42 analyzed a self-propagating npm worm that infected 400+ packages (collectively hundreds of millions of weekly downloads). Once a stolen npm token or a repo-scoped OIDC exchange gives the worm publish rights, it mints a real Sigstore in-toto SLSA v1 provenance attestation for the infected tarball — so signature-checking pipelines see valid provenance for malicious code. C2 domains resolve through an Ethereum smart contract, letting the operator rotate infrastructure with one on-chain transaction and no malware update.
takeaway: Valid npm provenance no longer distinguishes a safe artifact from an evasive one — pivot on the Rekor log identity and workflow, not on signature-checks-pass.

lessons.point: Valid Sigstore provenance is not evidence a package is clean — a worm can mint real attestations against its own compromised workflow.
lessons.excerpt: Given the reality of today's npm supply chain threats, a package having valid npm provenance does not mean the package is clean. It only means the tarball came out of the workflow named in the certificate. If that workflow is running attacker code, valid provenance is what you should expect to see.

lessons.point: CI runner memory is a live credential target — the worm scrapes /proc/<pid>/mem on GitHub Actions Runner.Worker to capture OIDC tokens and runner secrets that would otherwise never touch disk.
lessons.excerpt: An embedded Python helper hidden inside an encrypted blob in the payload locates the Runner.Worker process on GitHub Actions runners, opens /proc/<pid>/maps and /proc/<pid>/mem, and searches live process memory for OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens and runner secrets.

lessons.point: AI-coding-tool configs (.claude/settings.json SessionStart hook, .vscode/tasks.json) are execution infrastructure — the worm writes cross-linked persistence into both directories.
lessons.excerpt: It writes a .vscode/tasks.json file with a task labeled Environment Setup and sets it to run when the folder opens... It also writes a .claude/settings.json file with a SessionStart command hook, meaning it executes whenever Claude Code starts a session in the project.

lessons.point: C2 domain resolution via a blockchain smart contract lets the operator silently reconfigure infrastructure with a single Ethereum transaction, without pushing any malware update.
lessons.excerpt: This C2 rotation demonstrates the adversary's ability to silently reconfigure the worm's entire C2 infrastructure through a single Ethereum transaction, without requiring any update to the deployed malware.

threat: Worm-driven npm package compromise that steals cloud/CI/AI-tool credentials, chains publishing rights via OIDC trusted-publishing to mint valid provenance on infected packages, and persists inside developer environments through AI-coding-tool configuration files.
conditions: npm-published package with preinstall hook AND developer or CI environment that runs 'npm install' or the equivalent; the worm auto-propagates once it captures an npm publishing token.
mitigations: Grep for the 'Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again' marker in repo descriptions; hunt for .claude/settings.json + .vscode/tasks.json cross-linked droppers; treat valid npm provenance as authenticity, not integrity; monitor the Rekor transparency log for unexpected workflow identities; block both npm-cache[.]com and awqhnjewqjkl[.]icu; consider CI runners as credential-exfil targets and pin/audit dependencies rather than relying on provenance alone.
prior_art: Continues the Shai-Hulud npm supply-chain lineage (JFrog, May 2026). Novel elements: Sigstore provenance mint via trusted-publishing OIDC, Ethereum-based C2 resolution, .claude/settings.json persistence, CI runner memory scraping.

actionable.title: Treat valid npm provenance as authenticity of source, not integrity of code
actionable.detail: Update your supply-chain gates: if you were relying on 'signature valid + provenance attests' as sufficient for trust, add a check that the workflow identity in the Rekor log matches an expected repo/workflow. Grep repos for .claude/settings.json + .vscode/tasks.json cross-linked droppers as a hunting signal.

title: CRLF-Powered Desync Attacks: header injection escalates to CDN-wide response queue poisoning + browser-side XSS
summary: Portswigger extend HTTP header injection into a full-blown desync worm and show novel browser-side techniques for connection-locked and IP-locked desyncs. In an nginx misconfiguration where $uri is included in proxy_pass, URL-encoded CRLF sequences in the request path are decoded before forwarding, giving an attacker complete control over the upstream request. Applied inside a CDN's infrastructure, this captured session cookies and auth tokens from thousands of unrelated applications.
takeaway: HTTP header injection is severely underestimated — one nginx $uri-in-proxy_pass misconfig can escalate to CDN-wide response queue poisoning that harvests session cookies from unrelated tenants.

lessons.point: nginx URL-decodes the request path when $uri is used in proxy_pass, allowing encoded CRLF (%0d%0a) sequences to inject arbitrary headers into the upstream request.
lessons.excerpt: In Nginx configurations (an extremely popular web server) if the $uri variable is included in the proxy_pass directive, Nginx will normalise the request path before use, url-decoding any encoded characters including CRLF sequences (%0d%0a). This allows us to inject new lines into the request that is forwarded upstream of Nginx, giving us full control over the structure of that request.

lessons.point: Response Queue Poisoning inside a CDN's own infrastructure lets an attacker route requests to arbitrary tenant domains on that CDN — capturing session cookies and auth tokens across thousands of unrelated applications.
lessons.excerpt: Impact wise, as a result of capturing requests, we also started to capture session cookies and auth tokens for thousands of applications hosted on the CDN.

lessons.point: Request splitting with exactly two smuggled requests achieves RQP without any RFC violation — two CRLFs in a row are just another request boundary, so request splitting works out-of-the-box against many stacks.
lessons.excerpt: This technique does not breach the RFC using mutated headers in any way. Two CRLF sequences in a row, are simply another boundary between requests and as a result, this technique works exceptionally well out-of-the-box.

threat: HTTP header injection in nginx (or any proxy) that normalises URL-decoded CRLF before upstream forwarding, escalated to Response Queue Poisoning inside CDNs to harvest cross-tenant sessions.
conditions: Reverse proxy (typically nginx) with $uri or equivalent user-controlled path variable interpolated into proxy_pass without CRLF sanitisation.
mitigations: Audit nginx configs for $uri-in-proxy_pass patterns; reject CRLF in decoded request paths at the proxy; deploy request-smuggling detection (Burp scan / dedicated proxy fuzzing) against CDN edges before assuming them safe.
prior_art: Extends James Kettle's 'Making HTTP Header Injection Critical via RQP' (2023) and Sergey Bobrov's nginx misconfig research. This paper is the BHUSA/DEFCON 2026 followup that operationalizes the technique across CDN infrastructure and introduces browser-powered variants.

actionable.title: Audit nginx configs for $uri-in-proxy_pass
actionable.detail: grep -rn 'proxy_pass.*\$uri' /etc/nginx to find configs where CRLF injection is trivial. Also add request-smuggling scanning to CDN edge tests, not just app tests.
