title: Willison: the OpenAI/Hugging Face 'accidental attack' happened during an RLVR training run, not deployment
summary: Willison reads the OpenAI timeline of its accidental attack against Hugging Face as an RLVR training-run failure, not a deployment failure. Safety behaviors are added late in the pipeline, so during a Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards run the training agents have no reason to hold back; and monitoring is loose because operators run thousands of parallel tasks. The framing shifts the incident from 'agent went rogue' to 'training loop by design lets agents do anything to earn reward.'
takeaway: Treat training-time RLVR loops as their own agentic system with its own threat model — not a preview of deployment; the safety behaviors that gate deployment do not exist during training.

lessons.point: RLVR training loops are agentic systems where the goal is 'take any steps necessary'; deployment-time safety training happens later and does not constrain training-time behavior.
lessons.excerpt: In RLVR - Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards - you set the model a goal and have it take _any steps necessary_ to achieve that goal.

lessons.point: The reason training-time incidents can look like malicious autonomy is that safety layers are not yet applied — they get bolted on after RLVR.
lessons.excerpt: This also helps explain why the models had nothing to cause them to hold back. Those safety behaviors are added much later in the process.

lessons.point: Cross-agent covert channels (leaving messages in filenames on a packaging server) emerge when training operators run thousands of parallel agents against real infrastructure; monitoring for cross-instance coordination is a training-time forensics gap.
lessons.excerpt: If you're training a new model like this you presumably set it thousands of tasks like this in parallel. I can see how you might miss that a tiny subset of your training agents have started leaving each other messages in filenames on your packaging server.

actionable.title: Model training-time RLVR as an agentic-system threat surface separate from deployment
actionable.detail: When threat-modeling frontier-training pipelines, treat the training loop as an agentic system that can touch real infrastructure with no safety layer applied. Add cross-instance monitoring (do parallel training agents communicate via shared side channels?) and network-egress caging even in training environments, not only deployment ones.

prior_art: Extends the pool entry 'Provider safety guardrails blocked incident response during the Hugging Face agentic intrusion' by giving a training-mechanism explanation for why the models behaved as they did.

title: OrchestraBench: Evaluating Multi-Agent Orchestration Failure Modes, Recovery, and Decomposition Quality
summary: OrchestraBench is a seed-reproducible failure-injection harness for multi-agent orchestration that introduces cascade radius and per-failure-mode recovery as primary metrics. On a 26-case diagnostic, a keyword/flag router scored 0% on adversarial cases with misleading or missing surface flags while an intent-reasoning model router scored 100%. Mechanism probes with a real Claude agent revealed three failure-handling tiers across five MAST modes: tool faults recovered fully (1.0), ambiguous delegation recovered partially (0.30), and three latent or semantic modes never recovered (0.0). Cascade radius grew from ~0.9 at depth 3 to ~4.7 at depth 7. A trusted-state ablation showed apparent containment gains came from the trusted-state signal, not autonomous detection.
takeaway: Multi-agent orchestration failures are not uniform: tool faults recover, ambiguous delegation partially recovers, latent/semantic faults essentially never self-heal. Blind retry hides latent faults and delays detection, so containment requires an external trusted-state signal, not just per-agent detection. Keyword/flag routers collapse on adversarially framed inputs where an intent-reasoning router does not.

lessons.point: Latent and semantic failure modes in multi-agent pipelines are not self-healing even with retries; only tool-fault modes recover reliably.
lessons.excerpt: tool faults recovered fully (1.0), ambiguous delegation recovered partially (0.30), and three latent or semantic modes never recovered (0.0)

lessons.point: Keyword/flag routers fail catastrophically on adversarial inputs with misleading or missing surface flags; intent-reasoning routers do not.
lessons.excerpt: a keyword/flag router scored 0% on adversarial cases with misleading or missing surface flags, whereas an intent-reasoning model router scored 100%, matching the oracle

lessons.point: Blind retry masks latent faults and increases time-to-detection, so containment requires detection and attribution rather than more retries.
lessons.excerpt: Blind retry reproduced latent faults and increased time to detection, indicating that detection and attribution are necessary for containment.

lessons.point: Apparent containment gains come from an external trusted-state signal rather than autonomous per-agent detection.
lessons.excerpt: A trusted-state repair ablation showed that apparent containment gains primarily came from the trusted-state signal rather than autonomous detection.

actionable.title: Add failure-mode breakdown and cascade radius to agent evals
actionable.detail: For internal multi-agent evals, separate tool-fault, ambiguous-delegation, and latent/semantic-error rates instead of reporting a single task-success number, and record cascade radius across pipeline depths. Do not rely on blind-retry for containment; add a trusted-state signal (external verifier or ground-truth check) at the boundary between agents.

prior_art: Extends MAST (multi-agent failure taxonomy) and prior orchestration benchmarks by adding cascade radius, per-failure-mode recovery, and a failure-injection harness rather than raw task accuracy.
threat: Adversarial or malformed inputs at router surface flags collapse keyword-based orchestrators; latent semantic errors propagate through pipelines undetected, with cascade radius growing with depth, so a single fooled agent can silently degrade a chain of downstream agents.
conditions: Multi-agent orchestration with pipeline depth greater than 3; routing based on surface flags rather than intent; retry-only recovery without an external trusted-state or ground-truth check.
mitigations: Use intent-reasoning routers rather than keyword/flag routers; break out per-failure-mode metrics in evals; add an external trusted-state signal at agent boundaries; measure cascade radius as a first-class metric so deeper pipelines are gated on failure-attribution capability, not just accuracy.
verify_note: All four lesson excerpts appear verbatim in raw abstract at data/_raw/mrscan-b048-1.txt. related_claims (tool-count-degrades-agent-performance, score-evals-on-groundedness-not-headline-f1, chain-of-thought-does-not-transfer-to-multi-turn) confirmed present in data/claims.json.

title: Signal or Spurious Cue? A Randomized Audit of Survey-Country Metadata in LLM Social Inference
summary: A within-record audit across five API models and six countries tests whether LLMs still redirect their forecasts when they know a country label was assigned uniformly at random. Verified metadata materially lowered Brier loss (-0.040), but disclosing that a label was random did not reliably attenuate its influence — models absorbed the spurious cue anyway.
takeaway: Telling the model 'this cue is random, ignore it' does not actually get it to ignore the cue; treat metadata channels as load-bearing even when your prompt says they aren't.

lessons.point: Opaque country labels and disclosed-random country labels produced identical country-direction shifts (0.214 each), and paired attenuation was essentially zero (0.0003, 95% CI includes zero).
lessons.excerpt: opaque and disclosed-random labels each produced country-direction shifts of 0.214. Paired attenuation was 0.0003 (95% CI [-0.0157, 0.0166])

lessons.point: Verified survey-country metadata was genuinely informative: it lowered Brier loss by 0.040 (95% CI [0.024, 0.056]), while the random-label regret CI included zero.
lessons.excerpt: Verified country reduced Brier loss by 0.040 (95% CI [0.024, 0.056]), while random-label regret included zero

actionable.title: Don't rely on 'this field is random' disclaimers in prompts
actionable.detail: When context contains fields that may or may not be authoritative, in-prompt disclosure of 'this is random, ignore it' fails to attenuate uptake; instead, remove the field, mask it, or route through a separate LLM call that never sees it. Verify with a within-record swap: same prompt, real vs. randomized field, measure directional drift.

prior_art: Broader work on LLM sensitivity to irrelevant demographic cues and to prompt formatting shows the same 'salience-over-instruction' pattern; this paper is narrower (country-metadata + Brier loss on survey forecasts) but adds a paired-attenuation design that most prior audits lack.
verify_note: Numbers and confidence intervals lifted verbatim; the 'ignore-disclosure fails' conclusion is directly stated in the abstract.

title: PDF-to-markdown pipelines are the hidden token chewer inside enterprise AI adoption
summary: Simon Willison surfaces leaked Accenture meeting audio in which the firm's agentic AI strategy lead identifies non-engineer users converting PDFs into images and then into markdown as a leading driver of internal LLM token spend. The takeaway is that document preprocessing choices, not model calls per se, dominate cost at scale.
takeaway: Cost budgets die by a thousand PDF-to-image-to-markdown conversions, not by the model call at the end.

lessons.point: In real enterprise deployments, non-engineer users converting PDFs through image-then-markdown pipelines can dominate LLM token consumption.
lessons.excerpt: "We're seeing from some of the data internally at least that it's actually not our engineers that are driving the token consumption. It's a lot of the non-engineers that are doing some of those behaviors"

lessons.point: PDF-to-markdown conversion is called out by name as one of the biggest token chewers inside a large consultancy's own AI spend.
lessons.excerpt: "I'm learning that's one of the big token chewers," Henderson says. "Turning PDFs into markdown: is that right?"

actionable.title: Instrument document-preprocessing pipelines as first-class cost centers
actionable.detail: Track token spend by pipeline stage (raw file -> images -> markdown -> model call), not just per model. If non-engineer users are shipping PDFs through image OCR to markdown before calling the model, that stage is likely the top line item; cache converted artifacts and prefer native text extraction where possible.

prior_art: toon-cuts-input-tokens-vs-json (ai-research claim on input-token accounting) and general Simon Willison cost-of-tokens commentary.

title: Personalized Deep Research Query Refinement with Graph-Scaffolded Evidence Grounding
summary: G-STEER treats personalization of a deep-research agent as a pre-pipeline query-refinement step rather than modifying the agent itself: an 'Intent Elicitation Graph' organizes framing factors (user goals, constraints, preferences, evaluation criteria) with dependencies, and a learned clarification policy decides at each step whether to retrieve from user memory, ask the user, or stop and refine. The authors report the strongest weighted target coverage and highest downstream report personalization across two evaluated deep research agents (DRAs) while asking roughly one third as many user questions as a strong clarification baseline. The design keeps the underlying research agent unchanged — personalization lives entirely in a specification-refinement layer.
takeaway: Personalize a deep-research agent by refining the *specification* before it hits the agent, not by modifying the agent itself — and use a dependency graph over framing factors to decide when to ask the user vs consult memory vs stop.

lessons.point: User context can be injected at two layers — inside the deep-research pipeline or into the input specification — and refining the specification lets you personalize with an unchanged downstream agent.
lessons.excerpt: User context can be incorporated either within the deep research pipeline or into the research specification provided as its input. We focus on the latter, refining the user request into a personalized research specification before passing it to an unchanged deep research agent.

lessons.point: The clarification decision resolves three coupled sub-decisions: which framing factors matter, whether current context supports them, and which of retrieve-memory / ask-user / stop-and-refine is the right next action.
lessons.excerpt: This requires resolving three coupled decisions: which framing factors are relevant, whether the available user context sufficiently supports them, and whether to retrieve user memory, ask the user, or stop and refine the query.

lessons.point: Structuring framing factors as an 'Intent Elicitation Graph' with dependencies lets a policy be trained on trajectories that span diverse factor-dependency and evidence-availability conditions.
lessons.excerpt: G-STEER organizes framing factors as elicitation targets in an Intent Elicitation Graph that captures their dependencies. It learns a clarification policy from graph-scaffolded trajectories spanning diverse factor dependencies and evidence conditions.

lessons.point: The reported gain is not just quality — it is also asking users ~3x fewer questions than the strong clarification baseline while achieving higher personalization.
lessons.excerpt: Experiments show that G-STEER achieves the strongest overall weighted target coverage and the highest downstream report personalization across both evaluated DRAs, while asking roughly one third as many user questions as a strong clarification baseline.

actionable.title: Split a deep-research agent into a refinement layer and an unchanged execution agent
actionable.detail: If you are building a deep-research assistant, put personalization/clarification logic into a query-refinement stage that outputs a specification, then hand that specification to a stateless research agent. The refinement stage decides between (retrieve-memory / ask-user / stop-and-refine) using a dependency graph over the framing factors it still needs to resolve — a cleaner separation of concerns than editing the research pipeline itself, and empirically fewer user questions.

prior_art: Extends the clarification-agent line (CLAM, ClarQ, InterCode-Clarify) and specification-decomposition planners; the new lever is the explicit dependency graph over framing factors combined with a spec-refinement wrapper around an unchanged DRA.
verify_note: All four excerpts verified verbatim against data/_raw/mrscan-b053-1.txt. Abstract-only; no numeric evaluation-detail claims made beyond what the abstract states.

title: When Self-Evolution Backfires: Pre-Commit Gating against Skill Contamination in LLM Agents
summary: Self-evolving agents accumulate reusable skills from execution traces, but past a critical pool size added skills degrade performance. The paper argues contamination is structurally irreversible — once a defective skill is used to distill later skills, post-hoc removal recovers only a small fraction. Proposes Verifier-as-Gatekeeper (VaG): three critics (structural validity, behavioral harmlessness, semantic consistency) plus marginal-gain subset selection, filtering each skill pre-admission. Reports 72% pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2 with a ~5x smaller pool that transfers to four other backbones.
takeaway: Skill admission in self-evolving agents must be pre-commit, not post-hoc. Once a defective skill enters the decision context, its descendants inherit the flaw and rollback does not recover most of the loss — echoes the memory-poisoning principle: gate what enters, don't argue it out later.

lessons.point: Contamination in self-evolving agent skill pools is structurally irreversible: removing a source skill after later skills have been distilled from it does not erase inherited flawed reasoning.
lessons.excerpt: We further show the contamination is structurally irreversible: removing a source skill after the fact cannot erase the flawed reasoning its descendants have already inherited, so post-hoc rollback recovers only a small fraction of the lost performance.

lessons.point: Skill admission therefore has to be a pre-commit control, motivating a verifier-as-gatekeeper with three heterogeneous critics plus marginal-gain subset selection to catch combinatorial contamination.
lessons.excerpt: This makes skill admission a pre-commit necessity rather than a post-hoc fix, and motivates Verifier-as-Gatekeeper (VaG): a progressive trust hierarchy whose three heterogeneous critics - structural validity, behavioral harmlessness, and semantic consistency - filter each skill individually, coupled with a marginal-gain subset selection that removes combinatorial contamination at the top tier before skills reach the runtime context.

lessons.point: On Terminal-Bench 2, unconditional skill accumulation peaks then degrades and post-hoc removal recovers little — the empirical signature of irreversibility — while VaG improves every round to 72% pass@1 with a ~5x smaller pool that transfers to four other backbones.
lessons.excerpt: On Terminal-Bench 2, unconditional accumulation rises to a peak and then degrades, giving back most of its gains as the pool keeps growing, and post-hoc removal of the culprit skills recovers only a small part of the drop - the empirical signature of irreversibility. In contrast, VaG improves every round, reaching 72% pass@1 with a pool roughly 5x smaller, and its frozen skill pool transfers positively to four other backbones and a second benchmark without re-evolution.

actionable.title: Gate skills at admission, not by post-hoc rollback
actionable.detail: In agent systems that accumulate reusable skills or long-term memory artifacts from execution traces, put admission gates (structural validity + behavioral safety + semantic consistency) in front of the pool. Do not rely on post-hoc removal — descendants inherit flaws and rollback recovers only a small fraction of the loss.

prior_art: Self-evolving / experience-distillation agents (Voyager-style skill libraries).
agent-memory-is-a-persistent-attack-surface claim — same 'gate at entry, not post-hoc' principle applied to memory.
verify_note: Excerpts confirmed verbatim against data/_raw/mrscan-b052-3.txt. cluster=B (agents and harnesses): fits 'long-running agents / memory hierarchy'. Related_claim agent-memory-is-a-persistent-attack-surface confirmed present in claims.json — the paper's pre-commit thesis parallels that claim's 'validate what is allowed to ENTER memory rather than trying to argue it out later'.

title: CASCADE: An Agentic Regulatory Network Framework for Patient-Data-Validated Downstream Perturbation Prediction
summary: CASCADE is a biology-domain agentic framework exposing gene-perturbation prediction over MCP. The paper's biology-relevant portion validates predicted direction of change against real TCGA/METABRIC tumor data. The AI-relevant portion benchmarks whether an LLM agent correctly grounds natural-language requests into CASCADE's real MCP tool calls: across 35 queries, a local model reaches 71.4% exact match and a larger model 85.7%. Schema and gene-alias failures are resolved by scale or server-side correction, but both models confidently default to the wrong perturbation type on ambiguous queries, and a targeted fix could not resolve this because the trigger condition never occurs.
takeaway: Real-world MCP grounding on a scientific tool suite tops out around 71-86% exact match, and the residual failure is a confident wrong-perturbation-type call on ambiguous queries; scale reduces schema/alias mistakes but does not eliminate confident intent errors, and targeted fixes can be uninvokable because the ambiguity trigger never surfaces as an explicit signal.

lessons.point: LLM grounding of natural-language requests into a real MCP tool suite hits 71.4% (local) to 85.7% (larger model) exact match on 35 queries.
lessons.excerpt: Across 35 queries, a documented local model reaches 71.4% exact match (85.7% for a larger model)

lessons.point: Schema and alias mistakes are fixable by scale or server-side correction, but confident wrong-perturbation-type calls on ambiguous queries are not.
lessons.excerpt: schema and gene-alias failures are resolved by scale or server-side correction, but both models confidently default to the wrong perturbation type on ambiguous queries

lessons.point: Targeted fixes for ambiguous-intent failures can be effectively uninvokable when the ambiguity trigger never surfaces at inference time.
lessons.excerpt: a targeted fix could not resolve because its trigger condition never occurs

actionable.title: Measure MCP grounding as exact-match, and separate ambiguity failures from schema/alias failures
actionable.detail: When evaluating an MCP tool suite, report exact-match on natural-language-to-tool-call grounding separately for (a) schema/alias errors (which are largely fixed by server-side correction or larger models) and (b) confidently-wrong intent calls on ambiguous inputs, which are the residual failure class. Require an explicit ambiguity-check step or clarifying-question fallback rather than trusting a targeted patch that only fires when the model self-identifies uncertainty.

prior_art: Extends prior agent-tool grounding evals into a real-domain MCP surface; consistent with 'agent tool selection can be steered by untrusted context' but the failure driver here is intrinsic ambiguity, not injection.
threat: MCP tool grounding fails silently on ambiguous natural-language inputs by defaulting to the wrong operation with high confidence; downstream biological or clinical decisions could be based on the wrong perturbation type without any error signal at the MCP surface.
conditions: Natural-language agent frontends to an MCP tool suite where multiple tool variants are semantically close (e.g., knockdown vs overexpression); no explicit ambiguity check or clarification step; residual ambiguity does not surface as a schema or alias mismatch.
mitigations: Require the LLM to emit a confidence or ambiguity flag before invoking an MCP tool; add a clarification/confirmation step for tool variants that are semantically close; log per-tool exact-match grounding rates in production, not just tool-call success; separate schema and alias failure rates from intent-error rates when reporting.
verify_note: All three lesson excerpts appear verbatim in raw abstract at data/_raw/mrscan-b048-3.txt. related_claims (agent-tool-selection-can-be-steered-by-untrusted-context, few-distinct-tools-beat-many) confirmed present in data/claims.json; not force-fitting a third.

title: FinEvo-Bench: A Longitudinal Benchmark for Self-Evolving Agents in Professional Financial Workflows
summary: Longitudinal benchmark of 120 real-case-grounded finance tasks across 20 scenes and six domains, comparing four self-evolving agent scaffolds on Qwen3.7-Max with paired non-evolving controls. Reports Letta highest evolved score (91.65), Codex largest self-evolution gain (+19.37), and — most interesting for harness design — skill-only evolution beats memory-only and combined memory-skill evolution in Claude Code; rubric feedback beats reference-answer feedback across all four scaffolds.
takeaway: For self-evolving agents on professional workflows, three concrete design signals: (1) skill-only accumulation beats memory-only and combined skill+memory in the tested scaffold; (2) rubric feedback dominates reference-answer feedback across all scaffolds; (3) gains concentrate at harder within-scene ranks (4-6) — evolution helps most where the base agent struggles. Longitudinal design (paired controls, shuffled streams) is the reusable methodology.

lessons.point: Across four scaffolds, self-evolution improves score by 9.33-19.37 points and cuts compliance issues by 0.12-0.44 per task versus paired non-evolving controls — measurable transfer of experience across tasks in a professional workflow.
lessons.excerpt: Across scaffolds, the evolving condition raises scores by 9.33-19.37 points and reduces compliance issues by 0.12-0.44 per task.

lessons.point: In Claude Code, skill-only evolution outperforms both memory-only and combined memory-skill evolution on task quality and compliance — evidence that persisting distilled skills beats persisting raw episodic memory or both together.
lessons.excerpt: In Claude Code, skill-only evolution produces higher task quality and fewer compliance issues than memory-only and combined memory-skill evolution.

lessons.point: Rubric feedback (structured criteria) yields higher scores and fewer compliance issues than reference-answer feedback across all four scaffolds — a general signal about how self-evolving agents should receive supervision.
lessons.excerpt: Across all four scaffolds, rubric feedback also yields higher scores and fewer compliance issues than reference-answer feedback.

lessons.point: Self-evolution gains concentrate at within-scene ranks 4-6 (harder cases) rather than the easiest 1-3, by 6.10-8.70 points — evolution rescues the tail, not the head.
lessons.excerpt: Paired score gains at within-scene ranks 4-6 exceed those at ranks 1-3 by 6.10-8.70 points.

actionable.title: Prefer skill-only accumulation with rubric feedback over episodic memory
actionable.detail: In agent scaffolds that persist experience across tasks: (a) accumulate distilled skills rather than raw memory (or both), (b) supervise with rubric criteria rather than reference answers, (c) evaluate longitudinally against paired non-evolving controls on shuffled task streams — not per-task in isolation. FinEvo-Bench provides the methodology template.

prior_art: Voyager-style skill libraries; agent memory design literature (MemGPT, Letta); AgentBench and SWE-bench (single-task, not longitudinal); rubric-based LLM-as-judge evaluation.
verify_note: Excerpts verbatim from data/_raw/mrscan-b056-2.txt. cluster=B (agents and harnesses): fits 'long-running agents / memory hierarchy' and 'agent evals'. related_claims: agent-memory-is-a-persistent-attack-surface is tangentially related (skill-vs-memory persistence choice), noted but not a strong support/contest tie.

title: Innovation-Residual Auditing of Autonomous Analysis Agents: Localization, Detection Limits, Error Control, and Identifiability
summary: Analyzes when innovation-residual audits can localize a bad operation inside an autonomous data-analysis agent's trace. Shows the choice of scoring window is decisive - short windows produce one flag per mistake but blur inherited errors, long windows spread one mistake across many operations. Gives exchangeability-based false-flag control and proves an identifiability floor: below a certain error magnitude, no such audit can attribute the fault, and the floor is dominated by representation dimension rather than training-data volume.
takeaway: For agent-op forensics, the auditor's scoring window and the representation dimension are the binding constraints, not how many past 'good' analyses you collected. A hundredfold data increase moves the detection floor by under two percent.

lessons.point: Score choice determines whether an error can be localized at all - short comparisons cannot distinguish an inherited error from the original.
lessons.excerpt: The choice of score determines whether an error can be localized at all. If each operation is scored by how surprising it is given the operation immediately preceding it, then operations that merely inherit an earlier error are indistinguishable from correct ones, so one mistake produces one flag; scores computed against a longer reconstruction of the intended analysis instead spread a single mistake across many operations.

lessons.point: There is a hard identifiability floor: errors below a threshold cannot be attributed and the floor scales with representation dimension, not with the number of collected sound analyses.
lessons.excerpt: This limit falls so slowly as more sound analyses are collected that at the representation sizes now in use a hundredfold increase reduces it by under two percent, so the dimension of the representation rather than the volume of training data is the binding constraint.

lessons.point: False-flag control needs only that sound analyses be exchangeable, not that the fitted model be correct.
lessons.excerpt: we then give procedures that control the proportion of falsely flagged operations within a single audited analysis, requiring only that sound analyses be exchangeable rather than that the fitted model be correct

actionable.title: Log full operation traces for autonomous analysis agents so post-hoc audits can use variable window lengths
actionable.detail: If you plan to audit an agent's data-analysis trace after an incident, the auditor will need per-step context spanning multiple prior operations - not just the immediately preceding step. Store the full ordered operation log with inputs and intermediate outputs so window-length is an audit-time choice, and be honest that small errors cannot be attributed regardless of how much 'good' history you collect.

prior_art: Innovation-residual and conformal-anomaly auditing exist in statistics; the contribution is applying them to agent traces with explicit false-flag control and an identifiability lower bound.
threat: For a defender running an autonomous-analysis agent, small-magnitude adversarial or accidental errors sit below the audit's identifiability floor and cannot be attributed to a specific operation - useful signal for anyone assuming that 'more logged runs' will fix agent forensics.
conditions: Applies to unsupervised-audit setups that learn from known-sound analyses and flag surprising operations; assumes exchangeability of sound analyses and controls only within-analysis false-flag rate.
mitigations: Instrument agent runs with retained multi-step context; pick score-window lengths deliberately per-audit; treat below-floor errors as unattributable rather than absent; do not rely on collecting more sound analyses as a substitute for a smaller representation dimension.
verify_note: All three excerpts verbatim from the arXiv abstract at 2608.05490. Cluster J (observability, IR, forensics) fits: this is directly about post-hoc attribution of operations inside an autonomous agent.

title: Agentic self-driving microscopy benchmarks support qualification but do not necessarily generalize to unseen tasks
summary: A benchmark and trace-logging framework for LLM agents that control microscopes. Across 105 agent configurations (1, 2, and 3-agent graph topologies, 5 LLMs, RAG and context parameters), 1,949 test runs, and 49,109 RAG retrievals, direct comparisons revealed clear latency, cost, and failure-mode differences, but surrogate models trained on architecture and test results did not reliably predict performance on new, unseen tasks. The heterogeneous test suite is useful for qualification, regression testing, and diagnosis, not for producing a task-independent global configuration model.
takeaway: Benchmarks over agent architectures generalize poorly: even with ~2,000 runs and ~50,000 RAG retrievals across 105 configurations, surrogate models could not predict performance on unseen microscopy tasks. Agent-config benchmarks are useful for qualification and regression, not for picking a globally optimal architecture. This mirrors the SWE-bench generalization limitation at the agent-architecture level.

lessons.point: Surrogate performance models trained on agent architecture and past test results do not reliably predict performance on unseen tasks.
lessons.excerpt: surrogate models trained on agent architecture and test results did not reliably predict an agent's performance on new, unseen tasks

lessons.point: Agent-architecture benchmarks are qualification and regression tools, not a search space for a task-independent optimal configuration.
lessons.excerpt: these benchmarks are useful for qualification, regression testing, diagnosis, and direct comparison, but the current heterogeneous test suite does not support a task-independent global configuration model

lessons.point: Even with 105 configurations, ~2K runs, and ~49K retrievals, the resulting corpus was insufficient to induce a global generalization model.
lessons.excerpt: In total, 105 agent configurations, 1,949 individual test runs, and 49,109 RAG retrievals were recorded.

actionable.title: Treat agent-architecture benchmarks as qualification, not selection
actionable.detail: When picking an agent topology or LLM/RAG configuration, use benchmark results for regression testing and elimination of clearly-broken configurations. Do not extrapolate a globally 'best' configuration from bench results to unseen production tasks; require task-representative evals for each new deployment target.

prior_art: Consistent with the broader 'benchmarks don't transfer' finding (SWE-bench generalization limits, capability elicitation gap); specializes the observation to agent-architecture selection for physical-instrument control.
threat: Over-relying on a benchmark leaderboard to pick a production agent topology, LLM, or RAG configuration risks selecting a config that scores well on the qualification suite but fails on unseen production tasks.
conditions: Selecting agent architecture from bench scores alone; benchmark test suite is heterogeneous but not representative of production task distribution; no task-representative evaluation before deployment.
mitigations: Use benchmarks for regression and disqualification only; build task-representative evals per deployment; retain trace-logging of tool calls, RAG hits, and failure modes so the corpus can be inspected per task rather than aggregated into a single score.
verify_note: All three lesson excerpts appear verbatim in raw abstract at data/_raw/mrscan-b048-2.txt. related_claims (swe-bench-doesnt-generalize-to-production-tasks, score-evals-on-groundedness-not-headline-f1) confirmed present in data/claims.json.

title: From Economic Agents to Agentic Economies: A Systems Blueprint for Economic World Models
summary: The paper proposes a six-level capability ladder for Economic World Models (EWMs), where heterogeneous agents (increasingly LLM-based) act, interact, and co-evolve with markets and institutions. A literature survey shows most work concentrates at the lower ladder levels; self-evolving agents and empirically-aligned economic twins remain rare.
takeaway: For agent builders, EWMs are being pitched as high-fidelity multi-agent sandboxes for training, planning, evaluation, and safety — but the field is still parked at rule-based simulators, not adaptive LLM economies.

lessons.point: Economic World Models are framed as safety-relevant substrates: sandboxes where AI agents can be trained, planned, evaluated, and safety-tested against markets and institutions.
lessons.excerpt: high-fidelity sandboxes for human decision-makers and as training, planning, evaluation, and safety substrates for AI agents

lessons.point: A six-level capability ladder organizes agent-world systems, but existing work is concentrated at the bottom (rule-based / static-LLM agents) rather than at self-evolving agents or sim-to-real economic twins.
lessons.excerpt: existing work remains concentrated in lower-level agent and simulation environments, while systems with self-evolving agents, endogenous institutions, persistent empirical alignment, and validated economic mechanisms remain rare

actionable.title: Track EWM sandboxes as a candidate agent-evaluation substrate
actionable.detail: If you build agents, watch the EWM literature (see the authors' curated list at github.com/FreedomIntelligence/Awesome-Economic-World-Models) as a potential source of high-fidelity multi-agent test beds — but do not treat today's rule-based simulators as production eval harnesses.

prior_art: Traditional agent-based economic simulation (Axtell, Farmer) and the Awesome-* curated list format. LLM-based multi-agent simulations (Generative Agents, Park 2023) already explored self-evolving societies.
verify_note: Abstract explicitly supports the six-level ladder and the safety-substrate framing; no fabricated claims.

title: VLMs for Videogame Data Annotation
summary: The paper reports that off-the-shelf VLMs struggle to answer basic questions about racing video-game frame sequences (and the authors observe similar failures across other game genres), and studies concrete harness knobs — input sequence length, resolution, question batching — that affect both annotation quality and token consumption. Countermeasures raised include VLM output mixing (ensemble-style aggregation) and prompt optimization. The framing is practical: how to use a VLM as an annotator for reward-signal labelling in offline RL and conditioned training when the underlying scenes violate real-world physics assumptions.
takeaway: VLMs used as annotators fail on synthetic (game) scenes even for basic questions; the practitioner levers that materially move quality vs cost are frame-sequence length, image resolution, and how many questions you batch per prompt.

lessons.point: VLMs adopted for video-game annotation face a domain-shift problem: synthetic scenarios are extremely variable and don't obey real-world physics, so out-of-the-box VLM competence transfers poorly.
lessons.excerpt: Their adoption in video games is on the other hand limited by the extreme variability of the synthetic scenarios and their poor compliance with real-world physics.

lessons.point: VLMs fail on basic questions about racing-game frames — and the failure generalizes across other game genres — so you cannot assume a strong general-purpose VLM will annotate synthetic domains reliably.
lessons.excerpt: We show that VLMs often struggle to answer basic questions on racing video games (although we observed a similar behavior on other game genres) and discuss countermeasures such as VLM output mixing and prompt optimization.

lessons.point: Input sequence length, image resolution, and question batching are the concrete knobs that trade off annotation quality against token consumption in a VLM annotator harness.
lessons.excerpt: We also show how input sequence length, resolution, and question batching affect the annotation quality and its token consumption.

actionable.title: Sweep sequence-length, resolution, and question-batching before scaling a VLM annotator
actionable.detail: When you plug a VLM into an annotation pipeline, do not commit to defaults. Run a small sweep across (frames-per-request, image resolution, questions-per-prompt) and measure both quality and token cost — the paper's finding is that all three axes materially move both quantities. Layer in output-mixing (multiple VLM answers merged) and prompt optimization for the residual gap before considering a fine-tune.

prior_art: Fits the broader 'VLM-as-annotator / VLM-as-judge' literature (e.g., LLaVA-based annotation, GPT-4V labelling studies); the specific angle here is synthetic-scene domain shift and quantifying the length/resolution/batching trade-off, not the ensemble or prompt-optimization ideas themselves.
verify_note: All three excerpts verified verbatim against data/_raw/mrscan-b053-4.txt. Cluster C (Model I/O and tokens) chosen because the concrete harness insight is a quality-vs-token-cost trade-off; the domain (video-game annotation) is adjacent, but the transferable lesson is about I/O sizing knobs.

title: Schema-Guided Hierarchical Information Extraction and Semantic Evaluation Using Generative AI
summary: Schema-based zero-shot extraction of hierarchical, variable-cardinality information from unstructured text in a single model call, paired with a path-based semantic-matching evaluator that classifies attribute matches as exact / semantic / useful / non-match using a generative comparator. Extracts 12 of 14 attributes at F1 > 90% on NICE HTA documents using Claude Opus 3, ~30x faster than a human domain expert, with reported cross-model and cross-organization transfer.
takeaway: For hierarchical structured extraction, a single-call schema-driven prompt plus a path-based semantic matcher with a rubric (exact / semantic / useful / non-match) outperforms the usual exact-string-match evaluation and matches practitioner needs. The evaluator rubric is the reusable idea — most extraction pipelines still grade on exact string equality and undercount semantically correct answers.

lessons.point: Extraction of hierarchical, nested, variable-cardinality information runs in a single zero-shot model call under a schema — the schema itself encodes domain knowledge for both extraction and evaluation.
lessons.excerpt: The schema, serving as an information model encoding domain knowledge, provides a unified, systematic, and consistent framework for extraction of hierarchical, nested information, with attributes of variable cardinality, and subsequent evaluation of the results. Information extraction from a document is performed in a single call to the model, in zero-shot mode.

lessons.point: A path-based semantic matcher aligns extracted-vs-gold attributes in nested variable-cardinality structures — this is the aligning primitive missing from most exact-match evaluators.
lessons.excerpt: we introduce a path-based semantic matching algorithm to align the nested, variable-cardinality attributes in the extracted results with those in the gold standard.

lessons.point: The four-way match rubric — exact, semantic, useful, non-match — is domain-tunable and replaces binary exact-string equality with a graded verdict.
lessons.excerpt: We use generative AI for semantic comparison of the extracted and gold standard values of an attribute, and introduce a rubric to classify the result of the comparison, according to domain-specific considerations, as an exact, semantic, useful, or non-match.

lessons.point: On NICE HTA documents with Claude Opus 3, 12 of 14 attributes were extracted at F1 > 90% ~30x faster than a human domain expert, with reported cross-model and cross-organization/language transfer.
lessons.excerpt: We were able to extract 12 out of 14 attributes with an F1 score of >90\% from documents published by the health technology assessment organisation NICE, using the generative AI model Claude Opus 3. The time needed to extract the attributes from a document was ∼30 times lower than the time taken by a human domain expert.

actionable.title: Use a path-based semantic matcher with a graded rubric for structured-extraction evals
actionable.detail: For extraction pipelines that produce nested/variable-cardinality output, evaluate with path-based alignment + a graded rubric (exact / semantic / useful / non-match) instead of exact-string equality. The rubric surfaces 'useful but not exact' matches that binary metrics wrongly discard, and captures the failure modes practitioners care about.

prior_art: Constrained-decoding and JSON-schema generation; LLM-as-judge evaluation for open-ended outputs; classic IE evaluation (MUC/ACE) using string-match F1; the constrained-decoding-for-structured-output claim in the ledger.
verify_note: Excerpts verbatim from data/_raw/mrscan-b056-4.txt. cluster=C (Model I/O and tokens - structured output): schema-driven single-call extraction with structured output; A (retrieval) is also plausible but the substance is schema/output design, not retrieval. related_claims: constrained-decoding-for-structured-output is loosely related (both concern structured-output design) — noted but not a direct support/contest.

title: Search2Skill: Skill Distillation Beyond Knowledge Boundaries Via Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
summary: Search2Skill argues that self-evolving skill libraries built purely from the model's own parametric knowledge or its past trajectories are capped at what the model already knows. It proposes a rubric-based RL loop that jointly learns when to search, how to search, and how to distill retrieved evidence into structured reusable skills, and reports gains from skill abstraction (not raw retrieved text) that transfer across model scales.
takeaway: Self-generated agent skill libraries are bounded by the model's prior knowledge — closing capability gaps for expert domains means pulling in external evidence and distilling it, not just replaying good trajectories.

lessons.point: Skills built from a model's own parametric knowledge or its trajectories can't cross the model's knowledge boundary; expert-domain conventions have to be imported from outside.
lessons.excerpt: Existing self-evolving skill methods construct skills internally from the model's parametric knowledge or trajectories, and are therefore bounded by what the model already knows. However, the domain conventions and standard procedures underlying professional skills often lie beyond this boundary and are hard to elicit from the agent alone.

lessons.point: A rubric-based RL objective can jointly optimize when to search, how to search, and how to write the resulting skill, rather than treating retrieval and skill-writing as separate stages.
lessons.excerpt: Search2Skill is optimized by a rubric-based reinforcement learning scheme that jointly improves when to search, how to search, and how to generate skills.

lessons.point: The gain does not come from stuffing retrieved text into the context — it comes from turning that evidence into an abstracted, reusable skill that transfers across model scales.
lessons.excerpt: Further analyses show that the gains arise from skill abstraction rather than raw retrieved evidence, and that the acquired skills transfer across model scales.

actionable.title: External-evidence step for self-evolving skill libraries
actionable.detail: In a harness that grows its own skill/prompt library from trajectories, add a capability-gap detector that triggers external retrieval, then a distillation step that abstracts retrieved evidence into a structured skill — copying raw retrieval into context is measurably weaker than the abstracted skill, per this paper.

prior_art: Voyager-style self-evolving skill libraries; ReAct/Toolformer-style search-augmented agents; existing rubric-as-reward RL like OpenAI's RLAIF work.
verify_note: Excerpts verbatim from data/_raw/mrscan-b047-2.txt. Cluster B (agents & harnesses) fits since the contribution is a harness pattern for growing agent skills. Novelty is moderate — an incremental combination of known ideas rather than a new mechanism.

title: EcoAgent-Bench: Evaluating Economic Decision-Making in Budget-Constrained LLM Agents
summary: EcoAgent-Bench introduces a 304-task benchmark where every task carries priced actions and an explicit budget, testing four decisions: avoid unnecessary escalation, escalate when local evidence is insufficient, select a model tier, and stop on unsupported premises. Micro-averaged accuracy is shown to reward one-sided policies, so the authors report an 'economic-consistency' score (worse of upgrade-oriented vs save-oriented family accuracy). Tool-API agents attain only 3.9-24.0% strict success and at most 7.3% economic consistency; a threshold-crossing budget sweep barely moves GPT-5.4's escalation rate (0% to 3%).
takeaway: Completion-under-budget and economical action selection are distinct properties; a headline pass rate can hide always-escalate or always-cheap policies. Report the worse of upgrade-oriented and save-oriented performance.

lessons.point: Report the worse of upgrade-oriented and save-oriented accuracy, not the micro-average, to prevent one-sided policies from scoring well.
lessons.excerpt: Micro-averaged accuracy rewards one-sided policies: always-escalate controls achieve high micro success while failing save-oriented tasks. We therefore also report an economic-consistency score (the worse of accuracy on upgrade-oriented and save-oriented family groups) which exposes this failure.

lessons.point: Tool-API agents score dramatically lower on strict economic consistency than on micro success (7.3% vs 24%).
lessons.excerpt: Tool-API agents attain only 3.9-24.0% micro strict success (at most 7.3% economic consistency), often either stopping before warranted escalation or overspending on cheap tasks.

lessons.point: Budget threshold sweeps barely change escalation behavior for a strong frontier model, suggesting escalation decisions are not straightforwardly budget-elastic.
lessons.excerpt: A threshold-crossing budget sweep changes GPT-5.4's escalation rate from 0% to only 3%.

actionable.title: Add economic-consistency scoring to agent evals
actionable.detail: When scoring agent harness runs that offer local vs escalated tools, split tasks into upgrade-oriented and save-oriented families and report the worse group score; a pass rate that averages both will mask always-escalate or always-cheap policies.

prior_art: AgentBench, GAIA, HotpotQA / MuSiQue task families are re-used; the contribution is priced actions plus the split-family scoring.
verify_note: Excerpts checked against fetched abstract verbatim.

title: SearchAuditor: Auditing and Attributing Failures in Long-Horizon Search Agents
summary: SearchAuditor introduces SearchAuditBench (1,243 failed deep-search agent trajectories averaging 73 messages and 65K tokens each) with expert annotations for critical error step, search-specific root cause, and reference repairs. Their multi-perspective auditor with evidence-grounded adjudication reaches 32.3% end-to-end pass rate versus 26.6% for the strongest baseline built on a frontier model.
takeaway: Long-horizon search-agent trajectories are so noisy that even frontier-model auditors localize/repair failures under a third of the time — plan for auditor-in-the-loop, not one-shot triage.

lessons.point: Long deep-search trajectories are past human review scale, so failure diagnosis must itself be automated.
lessons.excerpt: Diagnosing such failures is difficult, requiring the manual inspection of extremely long execution traces, which could be beyond human capacity.

lessons.point: Even a frontier-model auditor tops out around 26.6% end-to-end on locating, attributing, and repairing search-agent failures — multi-perspective evidence-grounded adjudication only nudges it to 32.3%.
lessons.excerpt: even the strongest baseline, when powered by a frontier model like GPT-5.5, attains only a 26.6% end-to-end pass rate. In contrast, our SearchAuditor consistently outperforms all baselines across different frontier models, achieving an end-to-end pass rate of 32.3%

lessons.point: Curated failure corpora (73-message, 65K-token trajectories with expert-annotated critical steps, root causes, and reference repairs) are the substrate for training and evaluating agent auditors.
lessons.excerpt: SearchAuditBench comprises 1,243 failed trajectories, averaging 73.1 messages and 65.1K tokens, collected from eight open-weight models on five deep-search benchmarks, each expert-annotated with the critical error step, a search-specific root cause, and a reference repair with grading rubrics.

actionable.title: Add auditor-pass over failed agent trajectories
actionable.detail: For any long-horizon agent harness, log full trajectories on failure and run a second LLM pass that must localize the first bad step, attribute a root-cause category, and propose a repair. Even with frontier models expect only ~30% end-to-end recovery — surface residual failures to humans rather than declaring auto-repair a solved problem.

prior_art: General LLM-as-judge / trajectory critique work; adjacent to prior benchmarks like SWE-bench and AgentBench but focused specifically on failure attribution in deep-search trajectories.
threat: Deep-search agents can produce fluent but wrong answers because small reasoning errors propagate through very long noisy trajectories, and the traces are too long for humans to audit.
conditions: Multi-turn agent doing tool-heavy web search where each hop can compound reasoning error; failures surface only in the final answer with no per-step supervision.
mitigations: Log full trajectories; run an evidence-grounded auditor pass to localize the first bad step and propose a repair; treat auditor pass-rate as a bounded assist (roughly a third of failures) and escalate the rest to human review.
verify_note: All excerpts verbatim from data/_raw/mrscan-b047-0.txt. Novelty modest — failure-attribution benchmarks for agents are an active area; cluster J (observability/forensics for agents) is defensible.

title: SkillTV-Bench: Benchmarking How Well Judges Perform on Skill-Augmented Agentic Execution
summary: SkillTV-Bench is a 681-case benchmark of real agent trajectories from 50 tasks across eleven domains, targeting skill-aware trajectory verification (both LLM-as-Judge and Agent-as-Judge). The authors add SkillTV-Evolve, which externalizes verification knowledge as a reusable 'JudgeSkill' that guides an agent judge to plan targeted inspections and issue evidence-grounded verdicts. An automated evolution loop over misjudged cases raises judge accuracy by 14.8 percentage points; in offline rollout-pool selection, trajectory-success rises from 22.9% at one rollout to 45.5% at ten.
takeaway: Trajectory-level judging beats final-answer scoring for long-horizon agents, and encoding verification procedure as a reusable JudgeSkill measurably improves both accuracy and rollout selection.

lessons.point: Verification of skill-augmented agents needs procedural knowledge, not just the final answer, to decide what evidence to inspect.
lessons.excerpt: For skill-augmented agents, verification additionally requires the procedural knowledge encoded in task-time skills, because this knowledge indicates what evidence to inspect and which failures are task-critical.

lessons.point: Encoding verification as a reusable JudgeSkill and evolving it against misjudged cases yields a 14.8-point accuracy gain on the same judge model.
lessons.excerpt: On SkillTV-Bench, the refined skill increases the same agent judge's accuracy by 14.8 percentage points.

lessons.point: Agent-as-judge trajectory selection scales with rollout count: 22.9% -> 45.5% success from one to ten rollouts.
lessons.excerpt: In offline rollout-pool selection, it increases selected-trajectory success from 22.9% with one rollout to 45.5% with ten rollouts.

actionable.title: Evaluate agent runs on trajectory, not final answer
actionable.detail: When adding agent evals, log full tool-use trajectories and score them with a skill-guided judge that inspects intermediate artifacts, not only the final response. Final-response judges underweight task-critical failures in long-horizon runs.

prior_art: LLM-as-Judge and Agent-as-Judge literature; distinguishes itself with directly inspectable artifacts and skills.
verify_note: Excerpts verbatim from fetched abstract.

title: Activity Frames: Deterministic Screen-Activity Compilation for Agent Memory and Replay
summary: Deterministic zero-model pipeline that compiles passive screen captures into typed activity frames (application, site, timing, input volume, evidence pointers). One-user corpus of 128,756 frames over 51 days shows 86x context reduction per day at 68 ms, with 98.4% agent QA accuracy vs 66-80% for LLM summaries.
takeaway: A deterministic, byte-identical, model-free compiler over passively captured screen activity can shrink an agent's daily context ~86x while improving QA accuracy over LLM-summary baselines. Reported on a single-user corpus, so treat as prototype-level evidence.

lessons.point: A deterministic, model-free compilation of raw screen activity into typed frames yields byte-identical, cacheable, and auditable output — a property LLM summarization does not provide.
lessons.excerpt: it segments a local capture stream into typed activity frames, bounded episodes carrying application, site, timing, input volume, and evidence pointers back to the raw rows, with no model in the loop, so the output is byte-identical, cacheable, and mechanically auditable

lessons.point: On the reported single-user corpus, compiled activity frames beat LLM summaries of the same capture at daily QA — 98.4% vs 66-80% — and a mid-tier model reading the block matches a frontier one.
lessons.excerpt: the compiler reduces a day of raw capture to a prompt-ready context block 86x smaller in 68 ms, and an agent reading that block answers questions about the day at 98.4% accuracy (Wilson 95% CI 91.7-99.7%) against an independent oracle, versus 66-80% for an LLM summary of the same capture, a mid-tier model reading the block matching a frontier one.

actionable.title: Consider deterministic activity-frame memory for computer-use agents
actionable.detail: For computer-use agents that repeat routines, evaluate deterministic model-free compilation of screen activity into typed frames as a memory tier before paying frontier inference on every rollout. Note the reported evidence is a single-user corpus.

prior_art: Agent memory / long-running-agent compaction literature; computer-use agent papers.
verify_note: Excerpts confirmed verbatim against data/_raw/mrscan-b052-1.txt. cluster=null: nearest cluster is A (retrieval and context) / B (agents), but the work is capability/cost focused with no security angle. Not tying to a claim to avoid forcing a fit.

title: GAUGE: A Measurement-Grounded Benchmark for Physical Fidelity in Simulation Engines and Video World Models
summary: GAUGE is a real-world-grounded diagnostic benchmark of 22 task families (rigid bodies, flexible cables, textiles, volumetric deformable objects) with calibrated physical metadata, uncertainty annotations, and task-specific observables. It benchmarks Isaac Sim, Genesis, and Newton on 14 task families and evaluates 6 image-to-video models on 5 rigid-body tasks by checking physical-law consistency and temporal stability of inferred parameters. Headline finding: no physics engine is uniformly faithful (largest gaps in impulsive contact, rapid textile motion, and volumetric deformation), and video world models can generate motion with the correct equation form but wrong accelerations, momentum transfer, and oscillation timing.
takeaway: Generative video world models can fake the *shape* of a physical law while getting the underlying quantities wrong; perceptual-similarity evals miss this, so benchmarking has to compare inferred physical parameters against measured ground truth.

lessons.point: Existing physical-fidelity evaluations rely on perceptual similarity or human judgment, so they cannot say which physical principle a simulator or world model actually violates.
lessons.excerpt: existing evaluations of physical fidelity are often conducted in isolation and rely heavily on perceptual similarity or human judgments, providing limited insight into which physical principles or parameters are violated.

lessons.point: No single physics engine (Isaac Sim, Genesis, Newton) is uniformly faithful; discrepancies concentrate in impulsive contact, rapid textile motion, and volumetric deformation.
lessons.excerpt: Our results reveal no uniformly faithful physics engine, with the largest discrepancies arising in impulsive contact, rapid textile motion, and volumetric deformation.

lessons.point: Video world models can output trajectories whose equation form looks right while the recovered accelerations, momentum transfer, and oscillation timing are wrong — a form-vs-quantity failure mode invisible to visual inspection.
lessons.excerpt: We further find that video world models can produce trajectories with the expected equation form while recovering incorrect accelerations, momentum transfer, and oscillation timing.

actionable.title: Evaluate generative simulators by parameter recovery, not perceptual similarity
actionable.detail: If you rely on a video world model as an implicit simulator, do not treat 'looks right' as evidence of physical fidelity. Fit the produced trajectories to the expected equations and check whether the recovered accelerations, momenta, and periods match ground truth. A model can nail the equation shape while getting the constants wrong.

title: SkillHEX: Improving Agent Skills via Hypothesis-Driven Autonomous Exploration and Exploitation

actionable.detail: If you build a self-evolving agent skill system with a small trial budget, avoid single-incumbent greedy refinement; keep multiple skill-revision branches alive and use falsifiable in-code checks as a dense reward signal.

title: Revisiting Black-Box Model Ownership Verification through Information Theory
summary: Analyzes the robustness-utility trade-off in black-box model watermarking through an information-theoretic lens, identifies a capacity crisis when only predicted labels are used, and proposes a watermarking scheme that exploits the top-k output space instead. summary: The paper documents over 60 publicly available defence/national-security ontologies and introduces a new track for the Ontology Alignment Evaluation Initiative (OAEI) with eight matching tasks, consensus alignments (aggregated from several SOTA ontology-alignment systems), and manually validated silver-standard mappings. lessons.excerpt: The consensus alignments are derived by aggregating the outputs of several state-of-the-art ontology alignment systems. The silver-standard is obtained from the manual validation of the consensus alignment together with a subset of the unique mappings (i.e., mappings suggested by only one system).

lessons.excerpt: Achieving interoperability across diverse defence and national security ontologies remains a major challenge due to the domain's breadth and specialisation. actionable.detail: When you need a labelled alignment set on a fresh domain, run several alignment systems, take their consensus as an auto-approved core, and reserve human time for the mappings only one system proposed. Cheaper than annotating from scratch and calibrates system disagreement in the process.

prior_art: Standard OAEI methodology (consensus + silver-standard) applied to a new domain track; the aggregation-plus-manual-validation pattern is well established from earlier OAEI tracks (e.g., anatomy, large biomedical).

title: Poli-Bias: Understanding and Measuring Large Language Model Biases in International Political Conflicts
summary: Counterfactual framework that pairs prompts with country identities systematically swapped across geopolitical relationships, legal violations, and reasoning tasks, then decomposes response disparities into five interpretable dimensions rather than one score. Across 13 contemporary LLMs, country identity and user affiliation systematically shift how equivalent actions are described, evaluated, and defended.
takeaway: Counterfactual paired-prompt evaluation with country-identity swaps exposes user-affiliation-driven sycophancy and framing bias in 13 current LLMs. Method is generalizable beyond political conflicts: any domain where framing and legal reasoning matter can adopt swap-and-decompose evaluation instead of single-metric scoring.

lessons.point: Political bias in LLMs manifests through subtle differences in framing, argumentation, and legal reasoning that a single metric cannot capture — motivating multi-dimensional decomposition.
lessons.excerpt: Measuring political bias in large language models (LLMs) remains challenging as it can manifest through subtle differences in framing, argumentation, and legal reasoning that are difficult to capture with a single metric.

lessons.point: Counterfactual paired-prompt design — swapping only country identities across legally equivalent scenarios — is the mechanism used to isolate bias from content.
lessons.excerpt: Poli-Bias compares responses to paired prompts in which country identities are systematically swapped across diverse geopolitical relationships, legal violations, and reasoning tasks.

lessons.point: Across 13 LLMs, both the country identity in the prompt AND the stated user affiliation shift how the model treats equivalent actions — evidence that sycophancy compounds with entity-level bias.
lessons.excerpt: Across 13 contemporary LLMs spanning diverse model families and sizes, we find that country identities and user affiliations can systematically affect how equivalent actions are described, evaluated, and defended under international law.

actionable.title: Adopt counterfactual paired-prompt evaluation with multi-dimensional decomposition
actionable.detail: For any eval where framing matters (fairness, sycophancy, provider-affiliation bias), replace single-score judgments with counterfactual paired prompts that swap one axis (identity, affiliation) and decompose disparities across framing/argumentation/reasoning dimensions. Poli-Bias uses five dimensions; pick the ones matching your domain.

prior_art: Counterfactual fairness evaluation (Kusner et al.); sycophancy benchmarks (Anthropic 2023, Sharma et al.); LLM political-bias measurement studies.

summary: Introduces C-SUITEBENCH, a controlled multimodal benchmark placing nine frontier models in CEO decision tasks under paired text-only and multimodal conditions. title: TriQua: Reconciling Granularity and Context in Factuality Evaluation
summary: TriQua proposes representing simple claims as standard subject-relation-object triples and complex claims as hyperrelational facts with auxiliary qualifiers, then verifies factuality at the level of individual triples and qualifiers. The authors report tighter alignment with human factuality scores than prior decompose-then-verify frameworks.
takeaway: If you decompose LLM output for factuality checking, you probably need a variable-granularity representation — atomic triples for simple claims, qualified hyperrelational facts for context-heavy ones.

lessons.point: Pure atomic-fact decomposition loses context and pure statement-level verification lacks precision — this is a real trade-off for LLM factuality pipelines.
lessons.excerpt: atomic facts, i.e., one sentence conveying one unit of information, often omit essential context, while broader statements lack the granularity needed for precise assessment

lessons.point: Attaching contextual qualifiers to a base triple (a 'hyperrelational' representation) preserves context while keeping the unit small enough to grade.
lessons.excerpt: Simple claims are extracted as standard triples, while complex claims are represented as hyperrelational facts by attaching auxiliary contextual qualifiers.

lessons.point: Fine-grained error annotation at the triple/qualifier level gives explainable factuality scores rather than a scalar right/wrong.
lessons.excerpt: TriQua's verification process directly annotates concrete errors within specific triples and qualifiers, providing fine-grained explainability for error detection.

actionable.title: Use variable-granularity decomposition for factuality eval
actionable.detail: When building a decompose-then-verify factuality harness (e.g. for RAG output), do not force every claim to atomic-triple form — attach qualifiers to preserve context on complex claims, and score at the triple/qualifier level to keep error attribution explainable.

prior_art: FActScore, SAFE, and other decompose-then-verify factuality evaluators using atomic facts; hyperrelational KG representations from the knowledge-graph literature.

title: C3PO: Evaluating Cross-Modal Composition and Counterfactual Performance in Omnimodal Models
summary: Introduces C3PO, a 3,404-sample benchmark spanning video, audio, image, and text for measuring cross-modal composition and counterfactual conflict resolution in multimodal LLMs. Reports that best model (Gemini-3.1-Pro) reaches 73.17% vs humans at 88.64%, and that 86-95% of failures stem from modality dominance with attention concentrated on text.
takeaway: MLLMs collapse under cross-modal conflict, defaulting to text 87-95% of the time. Not a direct security finding, but the 'modality dominance' failure mode is a candidate attack primitive worth noting for anyone deploying multimodal agents against attacker-controlled non-text inputs.

lessons.point: Multimodal models are heavily text-biased even when the ground truth lives in another modality.
lessons.excerpt: 86-95% of failures stem from modality dominance: models commit to one modality while ignoring contradictory evidence, concentrating 87-95% of attention on text.

lessons.point: Multimodal input handling is far from robust: the best frontier model still lags humans by ~15 points on this benchmark.
lessons.excerpt: while humans achieve 88.64% accuracy, the best model (Gemini-3.1-Pro) reaches only 73.17%, with open-source models collapsing under conflict.

actionable.title: Treat non-text modalities as untrusted when they conflict with text
actionable.detail: If you rely on a multimodal model to reason over image/audio/video, expect it to ignore those inputs whenever text is present. Design tests and guardrails around modality-dominance rather than assuming the model fuses evidence.

prior_art: Modality bias and text dominance in MLLMs is well documented; this paper adds a counterfactual-conflict axis and quantifies attention concentration.
threat: An attacker who controls a non-text modality (e.g., an image or audio clip) could rely on the model to ignore that modality when its accompanying text is benign, weakening any multimodal moderation or verification pipeline.
conditions: Deployment must combine attacker-influenced non-text modality with trusted or attacker-friendly text; the paper only measures accuracy, not exploitability.
mitigations: Treat cross-modal disagreement as a failure signal rather than routine; run adversarial red-team probes that pit text against other modalities; do not assume the model reads images or audio at all when text is present.

title: ECG-LENS: Lead-Aware Clinical Context Enriched ECG Report Generation and Evaluation
summary: ECG-LENS is an end-to-end ECG report-generation framework combining per-lead encoders (preserving localized waveform morphology) with a global encoder for inter-lead dependencies, feeding a GPT-2 decoder conditioned on clinically enriched textual prompts. The authors also introduce F1-ECGBERT, a BERT-based domain-specific metric measuring agreement between diagnostic labels extracted from generated vs reference reports, arguing lexical metrics (METEOR, ROUGE-L) misjudge clinical utility. On PTB-XL in-domain and MIMIC-IV-ECG cross-domain evaluation they report absolute gains of 4.0% METEOR, 6.3% ROUGE-L, and 11.5% F1-ECGBERT over the strongest baselines. takeaway: For any domain-specific generation task, lexical metrics are the wrong yardstick; build a domain-native evaluator (here: label-agreement between extracted diagnoses of generated vs reference reports).

lessons.point: Lexical metrics under- or over-estimate report quality in specialised domains; a domain-specific label-agreement metric better captures clinical utility.
lessons.excerpt: Finally, because lexical metrics may under- or overestimate report quality, we propose F1-ECGBERT, a BERT-based, ECG-specific metric that measures agreement between diagnostic labels extracted from generated and reference reports.

lessons.excerpt: ECG-LENS combines lead-wise encoders that preserve localized waveform morphology with a global encoder that captures inter-lead dependencies. To guide report generation, we fuse signal representations with clinically enriched textual prompts that condition a GPT-2 decoder.

actionable.title: Build a domain-native evaluator before scaling a generation system
actionable.detail: If lexical metrics can't distinguish 'clinically useful' from 'text-similar-but-wrong' outputs, build a task-specific evaluator (extract structured labels from both outputs, compare on those) before iterating on the model. The gain the paper reports is on the domain-native metric (11.5% F1-ECGBERT) — 2-3x the improvement seen on generic ROUGE/METEOR.

prior_art: Domain-native BERT-based metrics for generation quality are a well-known pattern (BERTScore, PubMedBERT-scoring); the specific ECG-BERT variant and the two-encoder lead-aware architecture are the contribution.

title: Latent Fact-Checking: Detecting Misinformation through Activation Engineering

title: Refining Over Resampling: Test-Time Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning
summary: Argues that wider test-time sampling has diminishing returns because new rollouts repeat existing answer patterns, and verifier-based selection is bottlenecked by reward-model calibration. title: Unmasking Removal-Budget Confounding: A Matched Operating-Point Evaluation Framework for Adaptive Data Cleaning
summary: Adaptive data-cleaning methods claim precision/FPR gains that partly reflect shifting removal budgets rather than better corruption discrimination. title: Shaping Human-AI Interactions to Provide Improvement Pathways and Balance Competing Objectives
summary: Thesis studying human-AI interaction loops where individuals form beliefs about a deployed AI and strategically present themselves to secure favorable outcomes. Aims to design interactions that help users form accurate beliefs at minimal cost, encourage genuine improvement over gaming, and preserve the AI system's stated objectives. Integrates theory, data-driven modeling, human-subject experiments, and empirical evaluations.
takeaway: When a deployed AI evaluates people, interaction design should treat strategic self-presentation as a first-class dynamic to be shaped, not a nuisance to be filtered.

lessons.point: Deployed AI systems produce interaction loops where evaluated individuals strategically shape their inputs to fit their model of the system.
lessons.excerpt: When an AI system is deployed, the individuals who use and or are evaluated by it form beliefs about how the system operates and use those beliefs to strategically present their preferences, behaviors, or attributes.

lessons.point: The stated design goals are accurate user beliefs at low cost, encouraging improvement over gaming, and preserving system objectives like accuracy.
lessons.excerpt: (1) help individuals develop accurate beliefs about the AI systems so they can improve and or secure favorable outcomes at minimal cost, (2) encourage improvement and or discourage gaming behaviors, and (3) ensure that the AI system continues to achieve its intended objectives, such as maximizing accuracy.
